introduction.text: For almost 250 years, curriculum theorists in the United States have circled around the same essential question: What is the purpose of schools? The question sounds simple, but it never has a simple answer. The country is too large, too diverse, and too divided in its beliefs and priorities to settle on one clear purpose. Some people see schools as places for shaping moral citizens. Others focus on individual growth, workforce preparation, cultural literacy, or social transformation. The debates look different in each era, yet the underlying struggle repeats itself generation after generation.

In the early years of the republic, people like Thomas Jefferson argued that schools existed to maintain a stable democracy. Citizens needed enough knowledge to understand their rights and responsibilities, and the country needed a shared sense of civic life. Throughout the nineteenth century, this idea shifted toward moral development, particularly through Horace Mann’s Common School movement. Later theorists like William Harris pushed a more academic approach based on a fixed set of “core” subjects. At the same time, social meliorists such as Lester Frank Ward insisted that schooling should challenge inequality and help rebuild society. Even though their visions were different, they were all answering the same question using the beliefs and pressures of their time.

Across these changes, one pattern holds steady. Most visions of schooling, whether conservative or progressive, rest on the assumption that students must learn specific content. Reading, writing, math, and history have stayed at the center of curriculum planning for over two centuries, even as the world around schools has transformed. The country shifted from an agricultural economy to an industrial one to a corporate one, from print culture to digital culture to artificial culture, from local communities to global networks to neural networks. Despite enormous social and technological change, the basic subject structure and age-graded sequences of schooling in 2025 would still be recognizable to students from 1925, and even 1825.

That stability raises a new question for this moment in history. When information is accessible instantly, and when students grow up surrounded by constant technological and cultural change, does it still make sense for the purpose of schooling to be centered on content? Or is there a deeper purpose that makes more sense for the world students now live in?

I believe the purpose of school today should not be focused on what to learn – it should be centered on how to learn. Students need the metacognitive skills to understand themselves, to evaluate information, to work across differences, and to adapt when the world and their reality shifts again. Content still matters, but it should not be the foundation of curriculum design. The foundation should be learning itself.

This paper begins by tracing how the purpose of schooling has changed over time and how those shifts created the curriculum structures we inherit today. After establishing that foundation, I examine the frameworks educators use to modify curriculum, the structures used to sequence it, the limitations built into those systems, and the reasons those systems continue to dominate. My goal is to show why content-first curriculum models are no longer sufficient and why metacognition should become the new center of curriculum design.

The earliest attempts to define the purpose of American schooling were grounded in the political needs of a new nation. Jefferson, who was considered radical even in his own time, believed deeply that the survival of the republic depended on an educated citizenry. In his 1818 report on public education, he argued that schools should give every citizen the knowledge required to understand their duties, defend their rights, and participate meaningfully in public life[1]. He later proposed the first plan for free public education for boys in Virginia, a plan that met substantial resistance but still helped set the tone for schooling as a public good.[2]

As the United States expanded westward, Congress reinforced this civic purpose through the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. It declared that “religion, morality, and knowledge” were necessary for good government and the happiness of society, and that schools should be encouraged for that reason [3]. Of course, these ideals applied only to a narrow group. Early public schools mostly served white, male, Christian communities. Women, enslaved people, Indigenous groups, immigrants, and most minorities were excluded from the very definition of “citizen.”

By the mid- and late nineteenth century, the debate shifted from political stability to moral and intellectual formation. Horace Mann’s Common School movement framed education as a tool for producing disciplined, virtuous citizens. Mann insisted that mastering the “three R’s and Grammar” would not only uplift individuals but also reduce class conflict by easing hostility between the rich and the poor.[4] Around this same time, liberal humanists such as William T. Harris argued that a true academic curriculum should be grounded in what he called the “five great lines of study” which included math, geography, history, grammar and literature, and art.[5] Harris’s vision helped solidify the idea that a core academic canon was essential to becoming an educated American.

Not everyone agreed with this traditional structure. Lester Frank Ward, a figure Kliebard describes as a “radical visionary,” argued that schools should be used to reduce social inequality rather than preserve existing hierarchies. Ward rejected the emerging social-Darwinist logic of his time and instead positioned education as a collective project that could combat systemic injustice. Kliebard identifies him as a forerunner to the social meliorist tradition, which saw schooling as one of the central instruments for creating a more equitable society.[6] These competing visions — moral, academic, civic, and meliorist — coexisted uneasily and shaped the early evolution of American curriculum.

The early twentieth century brought another major shift, this time through John Dewey. Dewey reframed schooling as a social and psychological environment designed to organize meaningful experiences. He believed that students learn best when they engage in purposeful activity, and he argued that the school should function as a “miniature society” where children could practice the habits of democratic life. In The School and Society, Dewey emphasized that schools should prepare students to participate in a larger society that is “worthy, lovely, and harmonious,” which requires opportunities for collaboration, inquiry, and reflective thinking.[7] At the level of purpose, Dewey moved the conversation away from reciting information and toward cultivating adaptive, thoughtful citizens who could navigate a rapidly changing world.

Despite their differences, all of these models share a surprising through-line. Whether theorists emphasized civic responsibility, moral development, academic mastery, or social reconstruction, they built their visions on a stable foundation of content – or ‘knowing.’[8] Reading, writing, arithmetic, and history have remained fixed anchors for more than two centuries. Students today learn many of the same subjects, in many of the same ways, even though the social and technological world around them has transformed at a pace none of these early theorists could have imagined. This consistency raises a difficult question. Why does content remain the one part of curriculum that almost never changes? Why do frameworks and reforms pile up on top of it without altering the foundation?

This long history brings me to the central argument of this paper. The recurring focus on content is understandable, but it no longer fits the world students inhabit. As information becomes instantly accessible and as technology accelerates the pace of change, a content-first approach feels increasingly outdated. What students need most is not another variation of the same material, but a deeper understanding of how to learn in the first place. My goal in the next sections is to show how curriculum theory moved from foundational visions toward endless frameworks and modifications, and why this pattern reveals the limits of our current approach. The foundation has always been content, yet content is the least stable element of the modern world. If the purpose of school is going to keep evolving, the core of curriculum must evolve with it.

When examined closely, it becomes obvious how little genuine change has been allowed to happen. Most adaptations have been revisions to a structure Jefferson imagined centuries ago, often shaped by people who were never wrestling with the needs of today’s students. It is ironic that the same person who believed the Constitution of the United States should be rewritten every generation so that each era could shape the nation for itself, also outlined a school structure which has barely changed in 250 years. My hope is that by tracing this history, the curriculum proposal I offer later will not read as radical, but as a true restructuring.

renovations.text: After Dewey reframed schools as environments built around meaningful experience rather than containers for information, many educators tried to put his ideas into practice. The problem was that the implementation rarely matched what Dewey had in mind. In Experience and Education, he warned that unstructured activity can quickly become “mis-educative,” and he emphasized that the real value of workshops, kitchens, and school “occupations” was that they helped students understand “the relation of means and ends” (Dewey, 1938, p. 25). In other words, experience mattered only if it led students to think more deeply.

Instead, “progressive education” was often reduced to anything active or hands-on. Teachers added projects, games, and exploratory tasks, but the reflective piece — the part that mattered most to Dewey — fell away. This early misinterpretation created a familiar pattern in American curriculum work: when something isn’t working, we add a new strategy or framework rather than rethink the curriculum itself.

The result was not a redesigned school system but a layer of new techniques placed on top of the old one. Subjects, schedules, and structures stayed the same. Dewey’s broader argument about rebuilding curriculum around meaningful experience was simplified into a few classroom moves, and the larger system remained unchanged. This is where the framework era really begins.

bridges-bolted.text: As progressive ideas circulated, theorists began looking for ways to connect Dewey’s philosophy with the content-focused schools that still dominated the country. Ralph Tyler was one of the first to formalize such a bridge. In Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction, he argued that the goal of schooling was to bring about “significant changes in the students’ patterns of behavior” and that educational objectives should describe the outcomes schools aim to produce (Tyler, 1949, p. 14).

Tyler wasn’t trying to rebuild curriculum from the ground up. His goal was to help teachers organize whatever content their school already valued. His rationale made instruction more intentional, but it also reinforced the idea that content comes first and that frameworks help teachers manage that content more effectively.

This orientation shaped decades of curriculum reform. New frameworks emerged — more detailed, more structured, more aligned — but they all rested on the same assumption that content was the anchor and that the job of a framework was to make that content work better.

By the early 2000s, Wiggins and McTighe introduced Understanding by Design, which quickly became one of the most widely used frameworks in American schools. Like Tyler, they were responding to the gap between what teachers taught and what students actually understood. Their solution was backward design: start with the desired understanding, then choose the content and activities that support it.

But even UBD, which is thoughtful and reflective, still sits on top of preexisting content structures. Wiggins and McTighe make this explicit: they “offer no specific guidance about what the content of curriculum should be” (Wiggins & McTighe, 2005, p. 7). Their model helps teachers design better units, but those units still revolve around the subjects and topics a school has already selected.

This is the paradox of modern frameworks. They promise improvement, and often they deliver it, but they do so without changing the core structure of school. They act more like renovations than new construction: better organization, cleaner alignment, clearer goals — all within the same old foundation.

scaffolds-pretend.text: Across the twentieth and early twenty-first centuries, frameworks kept circling the same issue: a misalignment between teaching and learning. Dewey critiqued early progressives for confusing activity with experience. Tyler responded by grounding activity in objectives. UBD responded by grounding objectives in understanding.

Yet in each case, the curriculum sitting underneath these adjustments stayed largely the same. Frameworks addressed practical problems without challenging the deeper assumption that content was the primary purpose of schooling. This is why curriculum can feel simultaneously in constant reform and yet strangely unchanged.

Frameworks help teachers do their work better — clearer objectives, stronger assessments, more intentional design — but they do not redefine the purpose of school or the logic behind what gets taught. So the system evolves in small ways while its structure stays intact.

This brings us to the central issue: frameworks guide the use of curriculum but do not replace it. They can organize content, interpret it, or make its goals clearer, but they cannot explain why certain content matters or whether content should be the starting point at all.

Because frameworks avoid defining what should be taught, they preserve existing subject structures by default. The content remains stable while everything else — objectives, experiences, assessments, and language — shifts around it. This is why educational reform can feel energetic on the surface but unchanged at its core. Frameworks improve the delivery of curriculum without rethinking the curriculum’s purpose.
A helpful way to visualize this is to imagine repairing an old flagpole. You can tighten the screws, add supports, and repaint the base. But the pole itself never moves.

The next section looks at the deeper architecture of curriculum — the hierarchies, taxonomies, sequences, and organizational models that hold the school experience together. Dewey’s concerns about arbitrary sequence, his emphasis on organized experience, and the limitations of purely exploratory models are especially relevant here.
Understanding this structure is essential before imagining a curriculum where the foundation shifts from content to learning itself.

pyramids.text: What Dewey lacked was his ability to recognize and adapt structure and sequence into his philosophy. He never fully resolved how large-scale structures and sequenced learning would work within his philosophy. That gap made it easier for later attempts at ‘Deweyan’ scalability to skew his ideas. Curiosity and exploration should be maintained, but it is the metacognitive skills themselves – the how of learning – must be the primary consideration. Wiggins and McTighe, for example, lay out a hierarchical structure of six facets to clarify student understanding, with the final facet being rigorous self-reflection. I believe they have it wrong. Self-identity and reflection are not the end of a journey; they are the ongoing, foundational processes that determine the journey.

Hierarchies like this one often oversimplify a set of beliefs and ideas. In a self-deprecating attempt to organize the hierarchical structures themselves, I will be forced to commit the same crimes. However, this meta-analysis is critical for critiquing the field’s purpose of education and for proactively addressing a potential critique of my own hierarchy: sequence. The distinction of curriculum and framework has been noted above in detail. There is a third critical distinction to make: the sequence of learning.

hierarchy.text: The most traditional way to imagine an educational journey is as a straight line – a fixed developmental path that stretches over years of schooling. In curriculum theory, this shows up as a Hierarchy: a one-directional sequence in which each lower stage must be completed before the next becomes possible. The appeal is obvious. It’s clean, orderly, and gives planners a predictable map for an entire K–12 trajectory or even a lifetime of growth.

But this clarity comes at a cost. Hierarchies flatten the messy, dynamic, and highly personal process of learning into a single “correct” route, turning variation into deviation. Human cognition simply doesn’t unfold on a conveyor belt. Developmental and systemic hierarchies are everywhere in educational psychology. Jean Piaget’s model is the classic example. It proposes that children's intellectual capacity progresses through a universal, age-related sequence of four stages:

For its time, Piaget’s work was groundbreaking. He fundamentally changed how we understand children’s thinking. But modern research has shown that the stages are not as rigid as once believed. His model implies that a seven-year-old is confined to “Concrete” thinking, even though many seven year olds clearly engage in “Formal” reasoning when inventing stories or combining ideas in new ways. It fails the “test of scale”: real children don’t wait for their stage to “unlock.”
Ralph Tyler’s framework provides a different kind of hierarchy, one for the planner – not the learner. His four-step sequence offered a much-needed structure for curriculum design:

The issue is that Tyler’s framework locks the entire system into the first step: once objectives are chosen, everything else becomes downstream. It reinforces a content-first model that mismatches a curriculum oriented toward learning how to learn. Burns (2023) sharpens this critique by arguing that objective-driven curriculum designs like Tyler’s operate as “an apparatus of continuous judgment and surveillance,” where objectives and evaluation form a closed circuit that shapes what counts as legitimate learning. In this view, predetermined objectives do not merely structure instruction, they become what Burns calls “a technology of control that channels the conduct of learners toward preselected ends” [9].
Jerome Bruner’s early representational model can also be read hierarchically. His three modes form a progression from physical action to images to abstract symbols:

As a way to sequence content, it’s elegant. But as a model of cognition, it has the same problem as other hierarchies: it assumes a fixed linear climb. Many learners understand the Symbolic rule before they ever feel confident with the Enactive example, and sometimes the physical activity only makes sense after the abstract idea clicks. Bruner himself later moved away from this linear interpretation, arguing instead for a “spiral curriculum” in which ideas are revisited and re-constructed at increasingly complex levels hinting at a more cyclical and flexible model of learning.

Across these examples, cognitive, systemic, and representational, the logic is the same: learning moves upward. Lower levels are foundations; higher levels are destinations. Hierarchies are, in this sense, pyramids built on quicksand. They force a macro-structure onto a process that is inherently non-linear. And as we’ll see later, even Bruner himself moved away from this rigidity in his instructional theory, paving the way for the third model of learning: the cycle. But first, there is another sequence that builds from the bottom up: taxonomies.

taxonomy.text: Taxonomies are often confused with hierarchies, but they are technically different. A taxonomy is a classification system, not a life-long staircase. You can zoom a taxonomy in or out: it can describe a single lesson, a unit, or an entire course. It organizes types of behavior or learning objectives. In theory, it is flexible.

Bloom’s Taxonomy of Educational Objectives (1956) is the most famous example. Bloom and his colleagues described their taxonomy as a hierarchy only in the sense of “simple to complex,” noting that more complex objectives “include” simpler ones [10]. They also warned several times that teachers should not treat it as a rigid developmental sequence or as a ranking of what is most important (pp. 14–15).

Yet despite Bloom’s cautions, the taxonomy still behaves like a ladder. Once arranged visually with Knowledge at the bottom and Evaluation at the top, it naturally gets interpreted as a climb. This is not Bloom’s fault. It is a systems-design problem. Schools converted the taxonomy into a pyramid because pyramids are convenient. They tell teachers: “Start here, end there.” They tell curriculum designers: “Lower levels go first.” And they tell state standards: “Higher-order thinking comes later.”

The problem is that the real world contradicts. Rather than a model of how cognition actually works, Bloom’s taxonomy ends up functioning as a hierarchy of content manipulation, or a ranking of the operations students perform on subject matter. Each category is defined by the kind of task students carry out with the content, not by the actual mental processes underlying their thinking.

But thinking itself cannot be divided into levels this way. “Remembering” is not a low-level skill, it is the substrate of all cognition. There is no analysis without recall of prior knowledge. There is no synthesis without drawing on stored experiences. Evaluation is impossible without memory anchoring the criteria against which decisions are made. Memory is not a rung; it is the material out of which the entire ladder is built.

When a taxonomy treats a category as the “base,” it unintentionally frames everything above it as optional embellishment. But cognition isn’t built on a staircase. It is built on experience, and experience is built on more than just the highest stair. Without memory, none of the categories in the taxonomy are even conceptually possible.

Consider a simple objective for a gym class assessment: “Design a new exercise routine based on the four main movement strategies we discussed this unit.” Is “design” inherently more important than “remember”? Can a student design anything without recalling the strategies? And even if a student looks back at their notes, they must still remember where the notes are, how they organized them, and what the strategies meant.

This might seem like nit-picking Bloom’s taxonomy, but it exposes the central flaw of taxonomic sequence. The model does not account for the fact that memory shapes every cognitive act. Thought cannot exist without memory; thought is the conceptualization of past experience. Without past experiences, there is no memory; without memory, no thoughts; without thought, no awareness; and without awareness, learning becomes impossible.

cyclical.text: If hierarchies imagine learning as moving up and taxonomies imagine learning as moving forward, cyclical models imagine learning as moving around. These models view curriculum not as a ladder or a progression but as a recurring loop of interconnected elements. It is a structure that expands, revisits, and circles back long before it ever climbs.

Cyclical designs are built on the idea that different parts of the curriculum are interrelated and interdependent. Rather than positioning one step as the “foundation” and another as the “destination,” cycles allow any point to become the entry point. A cycle has no fixed beginning or end; the final node of one iteration naturally feeds into the first node of the next. In this sense, a cycle acknowledges that learning is ongoing, recursive, and shaped by continual return.

This framing also helps us return briefly to Jerome Bruner. Although his early representational modes are often read as hierarchical, his later instructional theory, particularly the spiral curriculum, moves unmistakably into cyclical territory. Bruner argued that ideas should be revisited repeatedly at increasing levels of sophistication, with each return reshaping the learner’s prior understanding. This is not a ladder but a loop: concepts deepen through repeated encounters, not by climbing a fixed set of steps. Bruner’s shift illustrates how even a theorist initially associated with linear progression ultimately embraced a more recursive, cyclical model of learning.

This does not make a cyclical model inherently “better” than a hierarchy or taxonomy; each serves different purposes. But cycles do highlight something important: the moment you are in determines what matters most. Whatever node a learner or designer is currently engaging becomes the “most important” one because it directs the next turn of the loop.

D.K. Wheeler’s model, proposed in the 1970s, is a classic example. His cycle moves from selecting learning experiences to aims, goals, and objectives, then through organization and evaluation, eventually looping back to the start. In Wheeler’s design, the aims and goals of one cycle directly determine which learning experiences should be selected in the next, reflecting how practice leads to new priorities and how reflection reshapes intention.

Shortly after, Audrey and Howard Nicholls offered another cyclical approach in Developing Curriculum: A Practical Guide. Their model begins and ends with Situational Analysis, emphasizing that curriculum making must always start with, and return to, the context in which learning occurs. They write that “changes should be planned and introduced on a rational and valid basis according to a logical process,” but the process itself is cyclical rather than linear. The context informs choices, the choices produce outcomes, and those outcomes reshape the context.

Cycles resonate strongly with metacognitive thinking because they make room for continual adjustment and reflection. Yet they still share one limitation with both hierarchies and taxonomies: in a cycle, influence flows primarily in one temporal direction. The next step is shaped by the previous one, but not necessarily the other way around. The past drives the future, and although you may loop back, the structure still assumes a forward-moving sequence.

In a knowledge graph (the 5th sequential pathway), every node influences every other node directly. The future can reshape the past as much as the past shapes the future. But cyclical models represent an important shift away from purely upward or forward sequences. They acknowledge that learning revisits itself, reinterprets itself, and grows through repetition rather than ascent.

orrery.text: If hierarchies imagine learning as upward, taxonomies imagine it as progressive, and cycles imagine it as recursive, then orreries imagine learning as radiant. An orrery is a learning structure organized around a core idea, with a constellation of orbiting concepts that contribute to, shape, and sustain it. Rather than asking, “What comes next?” the orrery asks, “What surrounds this?”

The defining feature of this model is its centeredness. A single central construct such as “significant learning” sits at the middle, and a set of interdependent domains revolve around it. Not every domain needs to interact with every other domain, and not every new idea transforms the entire system. What matters is that each domain has a meaningful relationship with the core, and the core is impossible without them.

This distinguishes the orrery from both hierarchies and taxonomies. It does not privilege one domain as the “first” or “highest,” and it does not assume sequential movement from one domain to another. Each orbiting concept contributes its own form of influence, but none dominates the others.

The clearest modern example is L. Dee Fink’s model of Significant Learning (2013). Fink explicitly rejects ranking or sequencing learning outcomes. Instead, he proposes that deep learning requires the integration of six interdependent dimensions:

These do not form steps. They are conditions, each one necessary, none inherently superior. Fink writes that the power of this system lies in the “synergy” between the categories; the idea that learning becomes significant only when multiple dimensions are activated in relation to a central purpose. This is precisely the logic of an orrery: the center exists because of the orbits, and the orbits matter because of the center.

An orrery model of learning is particularly useful when the goal of instruction is holistic synthesis, or cultivating a complex construct that cannot be reduced to a linear sequence. “Caring” does not logically precede “Application”; “Human Dimension” does not emerge from “Foundational Knowledge.” Instead, each shapes and reinforces the central idea in different ways.
This approach also has historical resonance. Several theorists implicitly used orrery-like structures even if they never labeled them as such:

Dewey’s conception of experience links knowledge, action, reflection, and social growth around the core idea of democratic living. Each dimension contributes to the central concept without needing to be sequenced.
Maria Montessori framed learning environments around the “prepared environment,” a central construct sustained by domains such as sensorially, practical life, independence, and concentration.
Nel Noddings’ ethics of care positions caring as the central construct, supported by relational, emotional, and contextual domains.

Urie Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems theory places the individual at the center, encircled by nested environmental layers—microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem, macrosystem. Each ring influences the center, but not all rings need to influence each other.

In all of these cases, learning is organized around a center of gravity. Instead of pulling learners upward or pushing them forward, the orrery pulls understanding inward, toward a concept that grows richer as its surrounding nodes accumulate.[11]

As a sequence model, then, the orrery offers a different kind of flexibility. It allows educators to design learning around essential understandings, with supporting domains that feed, enrich, or stabilize the central idea. It preserves conceptual clarity without enforcing linearity. It supports complexity without assuming universal connectedness. It is, in short, a model for understanding how multiple dimensions of learning contribute to a singular, meaningful whole.

knowledge-graph.text: In high school APUSH, nobody encounters slavery for the first time when they read Frederick Douglass or Olaudah Equiano. By the time students reach those primary sources, they have already accumulated years of experiences: early childhood lessons on ownership, fairness and sharing; elementary stories about early America; middle school discussions of conflict and power. Schema theorists such as Bartlett, Rumelhart, and Anderson have long argued that new learning is interpreted through this accumulated web of past knowledge. Schemata, as they call them, are interconnected structures that shape how new information is understood. As Bartlett put it, when people encounter new information, “the visual pattern at once ‘matches’ some already formed pattern” in memory (Bartlett, 1932, pp. 32–33). Rumelhart similarly argued that “the defining properties of schemata are that they have conceptual interpretations and that they support inference” (Rumelhart et al., 1986). Anderson extended this logic by showing that when a schema is only partially matched, the mind “creates further information to complete the match” (Anderson, 1983). New ideas are never processed in isolation; they are always filtered through an existing network of relationships, assumptions, and memories.

When a student analyzes a document written by Douglass or Equiano, they are not starting at the beginning of the topic. They are drawing upon an entire internal network of nodes (ideas about justice, race, power, suffering, freedom, and human dignity) to make sense of what they read. Schema theory tells us that comprehension is literally the act of modifying and reorganizing these conceptual networks in response to new information. In this view, learning is not a staircase; it is an ongoing restructuring of a personal knowledge graph.

Modern computer science unintentionally provides an elegant metaphor for this kind of cognition. In 2020, Stanford’s Knowledge Graph lectures described how large-scale AI systems represent knowledge as nodes and edges (entities and relationships) built to evolve as conditions change. Knowledge graphs are explicitly designed for environments where information, categories, and interpretations shift. They rely on schema evolution, where categories and relationships are redefined; view maintenance, where summaries must update as underlying facts change; and truth maintenance, where prior conclusions are revisited when their supporting information becomes outdated or disproven (Stanford, 2020). These systems assume continual revision, exactly the kind of continual revision we expect from students as they encounter new sources, perspectives, and contradictions.

Ironically, educational psychology has been describing human cognition in similar terms for decades. Ausubel’s theory of meaningful learning depends on integrating new ideas into existing cognitive structures. Novak and Gowin’s concept maps represent knowledge as networks of interconnected propositions. Rumelhart and McClelland’s connectionist models contend that knowledge is distributed across patterns of connections rather than stored in hierarchical categories (Rumelhart et al., 1986). Anderson likewise argued that “schemata are organized hierarchically according to a part structure,” where each schema can occur as part of another (Anderson, 1983). Connectivist theorists like Siemens go further, arguing that “learning is a process of connecting specialized nodes or information sources” (Siemens, 2005). In different language, all of these theorists reject the idea that learning follows a single upward or forward sequence. Instead, they describe understanding as an ever-changing web of relations—precisely the logic underlying knowledge graphs.

Thinking in these terms clarifies why this fifth sequence in my model is distinct. When students learn something new, they are not simply adding another “fact” to a folder. They are modifying the topology of their internal graph by adding nodes, strengthening some connections, weakening others, and sometimes restructuring entire regions. The process resembles truth maintenance (Standford, 2020): a student may discover that a prior belief about the benevolence of the Founders cannot remain intact after learning about Indigenous displacement or the economics of slavery. These systems assume continual revision exactly the kind of continual revision we expect from students as they encounter new sources, perspectives, and contradictions

Researchers studying children’s word learning provide concrete illustrations of this phenomenon. Bloom argues that “word learning is usually a process of mapping new words to pre-existing concepts” (Bloom, 2000). Experiments repeatedly show that children attach meanings to the features that strike them as most distinctive; when those features turn out not to define the category, “the concept appears to be acquired along with (or perhaps even because of) the word being learned” (Bloom, 2000). For example, if students are taught the word “zapar” and shown a picture of an elephant with 6 legs drinking water at a watering hole, the student might think zapar refers to an elephant with 6 legs. However, if the teacher then describes the picture as the elephant zaparing water, the student realizes that it actually is a synonym act of drinking water. This is cognitive truth maintenance: a restructuring of the graph when new evidence makes the old configuration untenable.

This model also maps directly onto the challenges of modern schooling. Students live in a world where content, expectations, and contexts shift faster than any previous generation. The “world” changes – technology, social issues, vocabulary, identities. The “requirements” change; what it means to be college-ready, employable, or civically competent are dramatically affected by global health crisis, AI, political tension, and so many other factors. The “sources” change; students oscillate between textbooks, podcasts, TikTok videos, academic journals, and lived experiences. These changes often undermine earlier assumptions, forcing learners to reinterpret or redesign their prior understandings. A linear model has no built-in way to handle this. A knowledge graph model expects it.

This also explains why, in this sequence, metacognition is not a top rung but the maintenance protocol. When students reflect, question their assumptions, source their evidence, or reconsider their interpretations, they are effectively inspecting and updating their cognitive graph. They are asking: What nodes are relevant here? Which connections no longer hold? What needs to be relabeled? What prior conclusions must be weakened or replaced? (Standford 2020) In this framing, metacognition becomes the engine of conceptual evolution, not the destination.

The knowledge-graph model also resonates with theorists who resist the idea of right and wrong pathways. Connectionist and schema-based traditions emphasize that different learners construct meaning differently because their networks differ. Two students reading the same text can legitimately arrive at two different interpretations without one being less “advanced.” The question is not whether they arrived at the “correct rung,” but whether their internal network is coherent, evidence-responsive, and capable of revision. A student whose understanding of slavery consists only of discrete facts—dates, names, battles—has a structurally weak graph, not because they are at a “lower level,” but because the graph lacks meaningful connections to economics, law, racial ideology, and contemporary inequities. The goal of curriculum, therefore, is to help learners build networks capable of continual transformation rather than guide them along a ladder.

That is the real power of the knowledge-graph sequence. It does not claim superiority over hierarchies, taxonomies, cycles, or orreries. Instead, it provides a structure uniquely suited to conditions of rapid change. Where hierarchies expect stability and cycles expect recurrence, knowledge graphs assume volatility. They treat understanding as something that must be rewired, reweighted, or restructured whenever the world demands it. This makes them not a more advanced sequence, but a more adaptive one able to absorb the evolving realities of modern life without collapsing under the pressure of constant change.

oversimplifying.text: Even with all the differences among hierarchies, taxonomies, cycles, orreries, and knowledge graphs, each of these models is still only a partial way of understanding how learning actually works. Human thinking is shaped by so many different factors—our prior experiences, what we pay attention to, the cultural expectations around us, our emotions, and the knowledge we already have. No single sequencing model can capture all of that. Because of this complexity, most school subjects end up being organized in two familiar ways: horizontally and vertically.

Curriculum theorists describe vertical organization as learning that builds over time, while horizontal organization is how topics connect within a given moment. These two dimensions form the classic “scope and sequence” used in most curriculum planning. Vertical sequences tend to reflect a hierarchical way of thinking (simple → complex), and horizontal scope assumes there’s always more content to add. Both approaches end up reinforcing the idea that learning follows a predictable path determined by the subject, the textbook, or the state standards.

This is why world history tends to start with the Sumerians and march forward in a standard order. It’s why math is taught as a climb: counting → addition → multiplication → fractions → algebra → geometry → ... Those sequences feel natural only because we’re used to them; they’re not actually universal truths about how students learn.[12]

At the same time, I’m not arguing that one model is superior. It would contradict my own position if I said there’s no single “right way” to learn and then turned around and claimed the knowledge graph is the “best” sequence. Each of these models has a purpose. In fact, they can blend. A teacher might organize a unit around a central idea (more like an orrery) while also using a loose progression of reflection or inquiry steps (more like a hierarchy or cycle). These structures aren’t mutually exclusive; they’re tools.

You can see the limits of strictly horizontal/vertical thinking when looking at actual curriculum systems. Exam systems like the Cambridge Curriculum often function as tightly linear models, with structures that assume a narrowing pipeline of high-performing students. By contrast, reform efforts like No Child Left Behind or Every Student Succeeds Act loosen the structure and emphasize access, but often narrow learning to what can be standardized and tested. One approach privileges precision; the other flexibility. Neither fully escapes the two-dimensional map.

These tensions also play out within individual schools. Compare an AP U.S. History course with the regular-level version. AP is designed around thematic learning and historical thinking skills—sourcing, contextualization, argumentation, and identifying patterns. Regular U.S. History often becomes more about coverage and recall because the pacing guide and assessments require it. The same subject ends up expressing two completely different ideas about what counts as learning.

All of this points to a larger issue: content is still treated as the anchor of curriculum, even when the stated goal is deeper thinking or metacognitive development. But content is constantly shifting—history gets rewritten, scientific ideas change, technology evolves, and social realities look different every year. If content is unstable, then a curriculum built around fixed content sequences is also unstable. These sequence models are not curricula; they are ways of structuring learning within a curriculum. Treating any one of them as the backbone of curriculum design is precisely what this paper is arguing against. A metacognitive curriculum would flip this: instead of building the structure around content, it would treat content as something students can plug into a cognitive framework at any point.

Oddly enough, math gives us a glimpse of this idea. We don’t expect students to start by learning every number. Instead, they encounter representative numbers and operations that gradually reshape their understanding. Let’s take a hypothetical journey through the structured mathematical education of a student named Armen. When Armen first enters school at age 3, he might be introduced to numbers and counting. First grade presents him an entirely different language – turning counting into equations. Later, multiplication demonstrates a new way organizing those counted numbers into groups and relationships. Fractions and mixed numbers in fifth grade require an even more fundamental rethinking of what numbers represent. These shifts aren’t just stepping stones, they’re reorganizations of the entire underlying concept. In high school, geometry and calculate not only build on the traditional axioms, but create a new system of organizing thoughts with similarities to algebra. In Armen’s statistic class, those numbers he learned so long ago are now able to predict the probability of events.

As structured and sequenced as math is, it is anything but linear. Underneath everything is set theory, which students never see directly. Then high school geometry switches to Euclid’s postulates, a completely different mathematical galaxy in the same universe. And logic-based math introduces yet another structure, one that’s about ideas rather than quantities. So even in the subject people assume is the “most hierarchical,” the structure breaks apart when viewed closely.

When you zoom in on a curriculum, hierarchies start to blur; when you zoom out, taxonomies break down; when you look across time, cycles make more sense; when you consider what everything revolves around, the orrery fits; and when you think about how students actually learn, knowledge graphs come closest to describing what’s going on. Each sequence model captures part of the truth, but none captures all of it. Problems arise when we pretend that a single structure can stand in for the complexity of real learning.

This critique is not meant to reject sequences altogether; it’s meant to show why we can’t rely on any one of them as the backbone of a curriculum. Learning doesn’t move in straight lines or neat circles. It shifts, loops, reorganizes, and makes connections in ways that no single model fully explains. Recognizing these limits clears the ground for the next step: redefining what we want a curriculum to prioritize, and how schools might structure learning around the way students actually think.

microscopes.text: If curriculum shows what schools value, assessment shows what schools are willing to call “evidence.” Ever since Ralph Tyler outlined his model in Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction, the official purpose of assessment has been pretty simple: check whether students accomplished the objective (Tyler, 1949, p. 104). However, when states and federal governments attempt to assess individuals collectively, they’re forced to choose an objective assessable across 55 million students.

In a one-on-one setting, objective design tends to allow for more flexibility which in turn provides flexibility in assessment. A tutor who meets with a student for hours each week can read the cues we rarely write down such as how a student explains their thinking, whether they hesitate, when their confidence drops, or how quickly they bounce back from mistakes. Even a single classroom teacher can generally tell which students understand something and which ones are lost.

The problem isn’t assessment itself. It’s what happens the moment we try to scale that idea beyond human relationships. One teacher can know thirty students well. A school can track patterns across a grade. But districts, states, test publishers, policymakers, and college admissions offices can’t rely on relationships. They rely on numbers. They need something they can compare across classrooms, cities, states, and eventually the entire country.

And that is where the logic falls apart. Sullivan writes that “validity is not a property of a test but of the use to which that test is put” (Sullivan, 2023, p. 119). An assessment that helps one teacher understand a student, may be completely invalid when used to allocate state funding or determine college readiness. Yet our system keeps insisting that one assessment can serve every audience. That insistence creates the illusion that learning is something you can compress into a single metric; the farther you get from the individual student, the more absurd the claim becomes.

one-key.text: No example captures the bias of assessments better than literacy tests. Literacy has become the national shorthand for comprehension, intelligence, readiness, and even, at times, moral worth. EdReports, one of the most influential curriculum review organizations, builds its entire ELA review system on literacy benchmarks. Their K–5 and 6–8 indicators require materials to align with grade-level reading, foundational skills, and text-dependent questions (EdReports, 2024). States use these same assumptions when adopting materials. Districts follow suit. And because the Science of Reading movement has reshaped literacy policy nationwide, the sequence of decoding → phonics → comprehension is often treated as scientific inevitability in policy and curriculum adoption debates (Castles, Rastle, & Nation, 2018).

On paper, the logic is seems approachable. If comprehension depends on phonics, and phonics depends on decoding, then the best way to measure understanding is through literacy. And if that’s true, literacy scores reveal exactly where a student stands. But what about deaf students who never learn reading comprehension through verbal assessments?

A deaf student who uses ASL may not process sound-based phonics at all. But that has nothing to do with whether they can understand a plot, analyze a theme, or interpret a character’s motivations. Plenty of deaf students can comprehend complex texts but do not “sound out” English words in the way SoR frameworks require. They can demonstrate comprehension by signing an explanation, retelling the story visually, or drawing a scene that captures the emotional core. All of these are legitimate demonstrations of understanding.
So if a deaf student can comprehend a story but cannot pass a phonics-based literacy test, what is the test measuring? It isn’t comprehension. It’s conformity to one communication mode.
This is exactly why Grant Wiggins pushes these questions be asked when designing assessments:
Could a student succeed on this assessment for reasons unrelated to understanding?
Could a student fail for reasons unrelated to understanding?

A deaf student fails phonics not because they cannot think, but because the assessment was never built for them. An emergent bilingual student could understand a story perfectly but struggle with English decoding. A highly verbal first grader might analyze a book beautifully in conversation but cannot yet write a paragraph. These aren’t failures of comprehension. They are failures of measurement.

If literacy were actually about meaning-making, then a child’s drawing of a rabbit after reading a rabbit story would count. A conversation with a teacher would count. A performance, a retelling, or a visual explanation would count. But the system cares less about comprehension and more about demonstrating comprehension in one narrow, English-based, sound-based form.

That is why the deaf student comparison matters so much. It reveals a truth the system tries very hard to ignore: literacy is not a universal measure of understanding. It is a cultural choice disguised as a cognitive necessity.

two-radios.text: When you strip literacy down to its essentials, something much simpler appears. Assessment is not really about phonics, rubrics, or multiple-choice questions. It is about communication. Every assessment, across every domain, asks the same question: Can the student communicate their understanding in a form the assessor recognizes as correct?

It becomes obvious outside of literacy. In math, correctness is mostly about reasoning and accuracy. In music, correctness is more interpretive. There are rules musicians tend to follow – such as avoiding parallel 5ths, adding leading tones in a mixolydian scale, the hertz per second a sound wave vibrates after plucking a string – but a violinists audition to her school’s orchestra will not assess the performance with sound measuring devices. The assessment will be based on interpreted feelings from more subjective cues – how the ether of sound is interpreted by the assessor. This would be similar to an assessment in math where the grade is based on the handwriting rather than the answer being mathematically correct.

However, subjectivity is not universal. Perhaps a student who plays a Beethoven piece slightly off-key in an attemp to represent Beathoven’s deafness might be demonstrating deeper insight than someone who plays it mechanically “right.” Whether the student “passes” depends on the teacher’s values, taste, and expectations.

That’s the part of assessment we usually gloss over: it’s relational. It depends on two people successfully understanding each other. It is shaped by culture, expectations, and communication norms. The assessor decides what counts as evidence. The student tries to make their thinking visible in a way that matches those expectations.

This is why the push to create “neutral,” “objective,” or “universal” assessments can feel out of touch. There is no neutral communication style. Someone always defines what counts. And when the system privileges reading and writing as the only acceptable forms, every student who communicates differently—deaf students, emergent bilingual students, autistic students, highly visual thinkers, orally strong but text-anxious learners—gets mislabeled as less capable.
The problem isn’t the student. It’s the communication mode the assessment rewards.

compass.text: Assessment isn’t something schools should abandon. It’s essential. But before choosing the method, we have to be honest about the purpose. If the purpose is to help teachers understand students, assessment must be flexible and human. If the purpose is to track progress across classrooms, assessments need shared criteria but multiple forms of evidence. And if the purpose is to compare millions of children across fifty states, then we should admit that we are no longer measuring learning – we are mostly measuring compliance with a communication code privileging the dominant mode.

Literacy as a dominant assessment marker proves how this can dangerous. Literacy makes it easy to pretend that we are measuring comprehension when we are mostly measuring fluency in one cultural communication style. It convinces schools and policymakers that disparities in literacy scores reflect student deficits rather than measurement defects. And it convinces the public that reading and writing are the only legitimate forms of thought, drowning out everything else students can do and understand.

My goal is not to attack literacy or deny its value. Reading matters. But its role as the primary measure of intelligence, readiness, and academic potential is far more fragile than we admit. We have mistaken a compass needle for a map, and then we built our entire sense of direction around it. We treat the needle’s fixed north as if it were the only direction worth walking toward. But students live in a world where the landscape changes, the landmarks move, and the path ahead is rarely straight.

A system that orients itself around a single mode of evidence cannot prepare learners for a world defined by multiplicity. A curriculum built around one north cannot teach students how to navigate when poles shift. If assessment is going to play a meaningful role in learning, it cannot define the journey – it can only help orient us along the way.
And that brings us to the next question: if curriculum is not content, framework, assessment, scope, nor sequence, then what is it?

intermission.text: I want to take a moment to proactively (and potentially retroactively) clear up any confusions. So far, I’ve said that curriculum theory has both drastically changed yet stayed the same. I’ve critiqued various forms of sequences and structures while complimenting them situationally on their own in a sequentially structured format. In a moment, I will make the claim that curriculum as a field is undefinable and fragmented yet orbiting around the same purpose.

This multidimensional approach is not meant to give you whiplash. It is meant to resist the idea that there is a single, stable “truth” about curriculum waiting to be discovered. It is meant to show that both the journey and the definitions are messy, and that complexity is not a flaw to be edited out. No two people hold exactly the same view of curriculum, education, or the purpose of school, and my own proposal is no exception. What I am offering is a curriculum concept that grows out of, and stays accountable to, other people’s perspectives rather than pretending to float above them.

curriculum-concept.text: By this point in the paper, we’ve spent a lot of time on what curriculum is not. It is not just a list of content standards, not just a scope and sequence, not just a set of assessments that pretend to measure everything that matters. I’ve argued that American public schools have often treated content as the fixed anchor while frameworks, sequences, and tests orbit around it. If the purpose of schooling is shifting from what to learn toward how to learn, then that anchor starts to look less secure. The next question, then, is not “Which content should we prioritize?” but “What do we even mean by curriculum if we take how students learn seriously?”

This question has never had a neat answer. As I write this, I am enrolled in a Foundations of Curriculum graduate course that was partially organized around six different ways of orienting theoretical constructions of curriculum: curriculum as Product, Process, Practice, Praxis, Political, and Personal. We studied “curriculum” as something slightly different each week: a technical plan with objectives and outcomes, a set of interactions between teachers and learners, a vehicle for justice, a form of reflective action, a political project about whose knowledge counts, and an autobiographical journey. We didn’t resolve the question “What is curriculum?” so much as multiply it.

My goal in this chapter is not to add one more official definition to the pile. I’m less interested in declaring what curriculum is in a universal sense than in paying attention to what different people seem to be trying to do when they use the word. The sheer number of “curriculum as…” options suggests that curriculum may not be a single object waiting to be named, but a set of decisions about what learning should be and how it should unfold. In the next section, I look more closely at that apparent fragmentation, not as a failure to be fixed, but as a clue to what is really at stake when we talk about curriculum at all.

fracture.text: From the outside, curriculum looks remarkably fragmented; the more closely you look at definitions, foundations, or groupings, the more it becomes a field that can’t quite decide what it is. The field’s major texts don’t exactly simplify things. In 1949, Ralph Tyler published Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction, a title that suggests the whole problem might be boiled down to a handful of clear steps. If only it were that basic. Decades later, William Pinar released What Is Curriculum Theory?, which might be one of the most honest titles available: a direct question wrapped in a very long, very complicated answer. There, he focuses on curriculum as complicated conversation and social psychoanalysis. In 2016, Ornstein and Hunkins summarize curriculum as “a plan for achieving goals” (Ornstein & Hunkins, 2016, p. 8). It can feel as though every time someone tries to “settle” the curriculum question, the conversation splinters into a few more versions of “curriculum as…”

Particularly in academia, there are strong opinions about what is and is not a curriculum. For example, many science education researchers will insist that the Next Generation Science Standards are not a curriculum, but many teachers and districts refer to the NGSS performance standards as the science curriculum.[13] In earlier sections of this paper, I have spent time analyzing many of the components that are sometimes conflated with curriculum itself: frameworks, assessments, sequences, and so on. A curriculum may not require all of these components, but simply modifying one of them rarely results in a genuinely transformative curriculum.

Viewing curriculum through the lenses of the 6 P’s opens the door to explore it as an influence on how learning is understood and organized. Viewing curriculum through Tyler’s and Ornstein and Hunkins’ lens allows us to explore it through action and intent. Treating NGSS as a curriculum tends to imply a definitional understanding structured around assessments and standards; those who deny its curricular status often view curriculum as a broader concept that cannot be reduced to a set of performance expectations. However, even people who subscribe to a particular definition rarely claim that their preferred lens is all-encompassing.

In later parts of my Foundations course, Dr. Green demonstrated how the 6 P’s are not mutually exclusive lenses. In some contemporary curriculum reforms, the role of the educator is what creates, determines, and designs curriculum. One role designated to the educator in a culturally relevant pedagogy–oriented curriculum is to plan and carry out instructional experiences that connect students to the community, state, nation, and world outside of the school (Howard & Rodriguez-Minkoff, 2017). Curriculum as Process, Praxis, Political, and Personal all apply here.

Rather than becoming preoccupied with the many differing interpretations of curriculum, it may be more productive to view this diversity as an indication of education’s inherent complexity. Perspectives on curriculum are shaped by a range of goals, needs, and experiences, which naturally leads to multiple understandings. In practice, curriculum is not simply a fixed document or plan to be followed; it is an ongoing process of dialogue and decision-making about the nature of learning, continually shaped by various viewpoints and priorities.

factorials.text: The fragmentation I have been describing is usually treated as a problem, a sign that the field cannot get its act together. But what if the fragmentation is not a failure of definition but a clue about the nature of the thing being defined?

When a teacher in Kansas and a teacher in New York City use the word "curriculum," they are not simply using the same word with slightly different connotations. They are pointing at different conceptual objects shaped by different students, communities, histories, and constraints. When Pinar speaks of curriculum as autobiographical journey and William Harris speaks of it as a fixed canon of essential subjects, they are not disagreeing about the boundaries of a single concept. They are operating in different conceptual spaces altogether. The word is shared; the concept is not.

This is not merely a linguistic observation. It points to something structural. Curriculum, as a concept, is relational. It does not exist as a stable object that different people interpret differently; it exists as those different interpretations, shaped by the positions and purposes of whoever is doing the thinking. The concept bends depending on where you stand, not because people are confused, but because the concept itself is that kind of thing.

If this is true, then the question "What is curriculum?" cannot be answered with a definition that holds still. Any answer will reflect the asker's context, priorities, and way of thinking about learning. The concept is not one-dimensional (a single definition), or even three-dimensional (a set of competing definitions arranged in space). It behaves more like a tesseract: a shape that looks different depending on the angle of perception, whose full structure cannot be seen from any single vantage point but is no less real for being perspectival.

There is another way to say this. A school's chosen curriculum reveals its true philosophy more honestly than any mission statement or test score ever could. The curriculum a school selects, defends, and organizes itself around tells you what that school actually believes about learning, about students, about knowledge, and about its own purpose. In content-anchored systems, where funding and reputation hang in the balance of alignment, the curriculum does not just shape school. It becomes school. The institution bends itself around the curriculum rather than the other way around. This is a problem not because curricula are unimportant, but because school is supposed to be more than a curriculum. When the two collapse into each other, there is no longer any room to ask whether the curriculum is serving the students or whether the students are serving the curriculum.

Content-anchored curricula tend to share a few family traits. They define success primarily in terms of what students can show about a prescribed body of content. Frameworks and pedagogies may vary, but their job is to support coverage and mastery. They rely on sequencing tools like pacing guides, course maps, and developmental progressions that treat learning as movement through a pre-arranged content route. They lean on assessments that serve as proxies for learning, using tests, rubrics, and benchmarks to stand in for much richer forms of understanding. None of these tendencies are inherently disastrous. Many meaningful, memorable classrooms operate comfortably inside a content-anchored design. The point is not that this type of curriculum is simply wrong, but that it assumes content will remain the most reliable organizing center for schooling. In a world where information, tools, and social realities change faster than standards can be rewritten, that assumption starts to feel less stable.

This brings me to the term I will use from here forward: contexture. Contexture is not a remedy. It is a reframing. It is a way of conceptualizing curriculum relationally rather than statically, as something shaped by context rather than handed down as settled truth. It is a way of admitting that we do not know everything. It is a way of looking at a school without first asking whether EdReports has signed off on its materials. It is a way of refusing to measure success by a single test, or by alignment to a pre-prescribed, inflexible objective, or by proximity to some imagined "normal" benchmark.

A contexture is not a plan, a sequence, or a set of standards. It is a woven space, an environment designed to hold and support metacognitive practice. Where a content-anchored curriculum asks, "What should students learn?", a contexture asks a different set of questions: What kinds of thinking are being valued here? How are students expected to relate to knowledge, as something fixed to master, as something to question, as something they co-create? Who gets to revise their own understanding, and on what terms? At the core of contexture rests ‘opportunity.’

In this framing, curriculum is not primarily about the teacher (what they deliver), or the learner (what they receive), or even the relationship between them (how they interact). It is about what thinking is in that space. It is about how thinking is structured, what it is allowed to become, and what habits it cultivates over time. A contexture provides cognescient opportunities: openings for learners to notice, shape, and take ownership of their own cognitive processes. The measure of a contexture is not coverage or mastery but whether students leave it more aware of how they think and more capable of thinking when the situation changes.

The framework I am building does not push content out of the picture. Instead, it shifts the center of gravity. Rather than organizing everything around what students should know at each step, it organizes around how students learn, revise, and take ownership of their thinking across whatever content they encounter. Content still matters, but it is no longer the anchor. The anchor is cognescience itself.

Accepting curriculum as contexture may do something unexpected for the field. It may allow curriculum theory to become more unified, more accepted, less easily dismissed or pushed to the margins of educational discourse. If curriculum is understood as inherently relational, then the fragmentation that has long plagued the field stops looking like dysfunction and starts looking like honesty. Different perspectives are not competing for the one true definition; they are each describing the concept from the vantage point available to them.

At the same time, at the level of the individual learner, contexture does fragment. It fragments goals, duties, responsibilities. It does not hand students a single destination and a single route. It removes certain constraints and replaces them with freedom, with wander, with endospective exploration. But here is the strange part: by allowing that fragmentation, by building it into the design rather than treating it as deviation, the fracturing stops feeling fractured. When exploration is the expectation rather than the exception, there is nothing to fragment against. The learner is not being pulled away from some "real" path. The path is the exploration itself.

This only looks like chaos from the outside. To an AP student whose assigned goal is passing a single test at the end of the year, of course the opportunities of exploration seem fragmented. They seem like distractions from the thing that actually matters. But that is only because the content-anchored system has already told that student what matters. Remove that prior assignment, and the fragmentation dissolves. All is one and one is all.
This is the definition of curriculum I am working with. It is not a universal definition, and it is not a rejection of other definitions. It is a reorientation.

If curriculum is relational, shaped by the positions and purposes of whoever is thinking about it, then the concept itself cannot be separated from the people who use it. The previous section argued that the fragmentation of curriculum theory is not a failure but a clue. Different perspectives are not competing for the one true definition; they are each describing the concept from the vantage point available to them. Accepting this means accepting that curriculum, understood as contexture, does not exist apart from its interpreters. It is not a thing waiting to be discovered. It is a space that forms and reforms depending on who enters it, what they bring, and what they are trying to do. The anchor is no longer content. The anchor is cognescience. But even that reorientation leaves something unresolved.

If curriculum bends depending on where you stand, then the next question becomes unavoidable: whose positions have historically won? The earlier sections of this paper traced how content became the fixed anchor of American schooling, how frameworks were layered on top without ever questioning the foundation, and how sequences and assessments reinforced a logic of coverage and compliance. That logic did not appear from nowhere. It was built by people, defended by institutions, and maintained by systems that benefited from keeping it in place. Reframing curriculum as contexture does not automatically undo those histories. It does not erase the structures that decide which reforms are allowed to scale and which are quietly dismissed. A relational concept is still dominated by certain relations.

This brings us to the question of power. If curriculum is shaped by context, then who shapes the context? If change is possible, then who gets to define what counts as change? The sections that follow examine how curriculum has been influenced, directed, and constrained by forces far beyond the classroom. Theorists respond to their eras; society absorbs and distorts their ideas; conservative and progressive movements push and pull against each other for control of what schooling is allowed to become. Understanding who moves curriculum is essential before proposing how to move it differently.

who-in-charge.text: One question that remains to this day is a difficult question to ask: How does change happen? When a theorist designs a new framework, structure, or ‘curriculum,’ do college professors begin right away to teach the next generations of teachers? Or is change in education just more of an echo of current opinions where change? Do curriculum theorists have power, sway, or influence at all, or do theorists just have ideas of the time that they're able to translate into writing? I believe the answer is both because society was heading in that direction, and because theorists’ are valued as authorities when designing a curriculum.

John Dewey’s publishing journey predates the Spanish-American War – a war generally thrown in to a broader unit and tossed aside by US history curriculums. This War marked a major turning point in the global standing of the United States. At this point, the entirety of the “unclaimed”[14] Western Hemisphere had been annexed by the United States or neighboring European-originated nations. This wasn’t satisfying enough for Americans, so they upgraded their tactics to imperialism. After pushing Europe mostly out of the West, and defeating Spain in the Spanish-American War, the United States stepped up to the rank of global partner.

Industrialization had spread across the states as the dominant economic opportunity for the working class by the end of the 19th century. Wartime manufacturing propelled the economy, benefiting the rich and powerful investors and manufacturers. By the turn of the century, the wealth gap continued to grow, and with it did power and corruption. Our industrial powerhouse made our presence indispensable when the British called on our help to fight the Germans in The Great War. Two years into US involvement, Dewey publishes Democracy and Education where he modernizes Jefferson’s citizenry purpose of education. In Dewey’s view, the purpose of education is to foster a continuously adapting and evolving democratic society where individuals are educated to participate in and contribute to their community.

tides.text: Dewey was a product of the progressive era. His career began at a time of industrialization, the beginning of automation, and a multitude of reform. This era saw change across all fields. American historians of the era transitioned their framing of the early republic to call out the greed and selfishness of the Founding Fathers – the first of this type of rhetoric from prominent historians.[15] Women’s suffrage was sprawling with determined female fighters leading to one of the four amendments to the Constitution in less than a decade. Jazz music introduced a blend and ownership of art and expression by a suppressed group of people during the Harlem Renaissance. This was indeed a progressive era of change and reformation.

Unfortunately for Dewey, his influence didn’t come early enough; adaptation was thrust on Americans. Corruption overpowered success, and in a dust storm of bad timing, the gold plating of the US economy washed away. After the tumult of the Great Depression and the Second World War, nationalism began to shroud the complexities and nuances of curriculum. Very steadily over the next few decades, the liberal humanists reclaimed the prominence of accessible curriculum, but the economic backdrop had fundamentally changed. The industrial economy that birthed Dewey was dying, giving way after World War II to the Corporate Age. In this new era of managerial hierarchies and specialized roles, the messy, organic community Dewey envisioned was increasingly viewed as insufficient. The educational landscape shifted from a focus on the child’s natural "growth" to a demand for measurable results and systemic efficiency.

corporate.text: The Corporate Era is a very interesting narrative of US history largely unexplored by traditional historians. When the US government began breaking out the robber barons’ monopolies, the Rockefellers knew their strategy had to switch. A monopoly controls only one sector, but public education has the power to control knowledge. John D. Rockefeller’s son, also named John, created the General Education Board, one that provided more funding for US public education than the entire federal government for decades following WWI. The university where Dewey studied, the university where he taught, and the Lincoln School that assumed Dewey’s philosophies were all funded by the Rockefeller’s Board.

After WWI, corruption became fueled not by outright takeovers, but by subtle complex deals. This new era required a new architectural logic, which arrived in 1949 with Ralph Tyler. Tyler didn't just offer a philosophy; he offered a "rationale" – a word he uses repeatedly to describe a "systematic attack" on the problems of curriculum making.[16] Tyler argued that because contemporary life is "so complex" and "continually changing," educators could no longer afford to "waste the time of students" on learning things that were no longer significant.[17] The intuitive, ‘hit-or-miss judgment’ of the past was no longer.

Tyler represents the perfect case study of the reciprocal "give-and-take" relationship between theorist and society. His intent was to create a balanced, pragmatic framework where objectives weren't just guessed at, but derived from three distinct sources: "Studies of the Learners Themselves," "Studies of Contemporary Life," and "Suggestions About Objectives from Subject Specialists.” He explicitly warned that "no single source of information is adequate" to provide a basis for wise decisions, even arguing that a "comprehensive philosophy of education" was necessary to screen these objectives, ensuring they weren't just contradictory lists of facts (Tyler, 1949, pp. 4, 5).

However, the mainstream curriculum (echoing the accelerating corporate obsession with efficiency) did something else. The GEB provided the funding for Tyler to publish his research but only adopted his objective-first framework while ignoring his insistence on philosophical balance. Schools had no choice but to co-opt his tool or lose funding due to legislation lobbied by the GEB. This now meant that no school would receive funding without filling in the 'objectives' primarily with the views of "Subject Specialists," which Tyler himself noted was already the "source of objectives most commonly used in typical schools" (Tyler, 1949, p. 25).

This demonstrates how a theorist (Tyler) offered a holistic rationale, but society (the new Corporate structure) took his mechanical framework and gave it a different purpose, bending the theory to fit a need for standardization. It also demonstrates again how a theorist was influenced by his place in time. Tyler did not invent the obsession with efficiency but merely codified it, responding to a society that had "laid upon the schools" a burden of "tremendous increase in knowledge" that could no longer be managed by the "older and slower" traditions of the past (Tyler, 1949, pp. 16–17). Whether intentional or not, designing assessments around the primarily set objectives mimics an optimized, efficient workstream.
The "Tyler Rationale" became a synonym for rigid objective-setting, proving that curriculum, theorists, and society are in a constant, reciprocal, and often distorting relationship.

gender-reform.text: The Corporate Era reinforced a societal norm of efficiency, clarity, and optimization. Because of this, measurement was more structured and consistent. Job requirements remained as narrow as they were in the Industrial Era, and measurements of skill were told to you in the form of a pay check. The 60’s introduced another score of counterculture movement, similar to that of the progressive era a half century before. For the first time in US society, students themselves became drivers of societal change. The landmark Brown v. Board of Education case was not spearheaded by someone out of school, nor was it spearheaded by a political leader – it was spearheaded because of an actual student.
