This student and her family, with the help and support of the ACLU, eventually led to the President sending his national guard to Arkansas to escort the student to school safely. This fits into a much broader theme of the counterculture movement. The ideas of race were shifting. Fear of equality and change fueled debates and protests throughout politics, society, and education.

Action took place at higher levels of education as well. A number of colleges began to speak out against their country, something that would have disrupted the entirety of Harvard, Yale, or William and Mary decades ago. Activists spoke out against race, gender, and sexuality inequality, the Vietnam War, and the very identity of the United States. The GEB dissolved and David Rockefeller founded the Trilateral Commission, instituting globalist priorities. Tension between Social Meliorists and Liberal Humanists rose and vied for dominance, polarizing parts of the nation.

Why was this happening? Because a sense of uniformity was emerging. A sense of right and wrong, fair and unfair, important and unimportant. This right and wrong made it easier to spot differences and discrepancies; it trained you to look for what’s different from each other rather than what’s similar. For instance, was it fair that a woman who did the exact same job as a man get rewarded for her success less? Does that mean she is inferior? We can watch the work they complete, they measured the same, but are rewarded differently. The ideals of corporate America swept through society. Measuring a person’s worth against another became easier than ever. And schools reflected this.

Curriculum dominance began to fracture. No longer did one philosophy control the way schools functioned. Ironically, as curriculum shifts away from the glorification and nationalism of US history, curriculum itself is more politically swayed than Jefferson, Mann, or Dewey would have suggested. This push and pull relationship between many powerful branches make this a difficult analysis. Should teachers be forced to align their lessons with that based in their course textbook? Should a single company be allowed to design textbooks for more than half of all students? Should those same textbook companies receive funding from global corporations?

When examining how change in curriculum is influenced, the answer does not lie in a specific “who” or “what.” Rather, a symbiotic network of philosophies and ideologies push and pull at each other pressuring change or resistance by those in different circumstances. When it comes down to it, everyone indirectly affects change in curriculum by the influence they have on others; yet ones influence is limited by their experience. I will attempt to demonstrate this push and pull nature of society, educators, theorists, and students by presenting the documented philosophies with the greatest influence on change in the current day.

right-way.text: If Tyler reveals the mechanisms through which curriculum responds to pressure from society, the profession, and local practice, Michael Apple pushes further: who governs those "common sense" mechanisms, and whose interests do they serve? For Apple, curriculum is never a neutral list of facts. It is a political project that selects some knowledge as normal, hides other knowledge as marginal, and then treats those choices as common sense.[18] The question underneath his entire analysis is the same one driving this chapter: not just what is taught, but who has the power to define what teaching is for.

Apple argues that in our current moment, that power is largely in conservative hands.[19] He calls the dominant project “conservative modernization” and shows how it knots together four anchors – markets, standards, God, and inequality – into a single common sense about schooling. These anchors don’t just describe the system, they steer it. When markets become the natural language of education, reform only sounds legitimate if it promises choice, efficiency, or “return on investment.” When standards and test scores are treated as the only serious evidence, any proposal that cannot be translated into measurable outcomes is quietly dismissed. When religious nationalism and “traditional values” are framed as the moral center, questions about race, gender, or power are easily recast as distractions from the “basics.” Inequality, in this arrangement, does not appear as something designed; it shows up as the predictable result of individual effort in a competitive system (Apple, 2005).

The important point for my argument is not that conservatives have strong opinions, that has always been true, but that they sit at the choke points of change. Apple’s coalition of neoliberals, neoconservatives, authoritarian populists, and managerial professionals may disagree on details, but together they control the levers that decide which reforms can scale: state standards, textbook adoptions, testing regimes, teacher evaluation systems, accountability policies (Apple, 2005). They design the metrics, write the rules, and manage the data dashboards that define what “improvement” even means. In Apple’s words, they have “engaged in a vast social and ideological project”[20] to redefine the basic categories of schooling: what counts as achievement, what counts as responsibility, what counts as democracy. Once those categories are in place, whole swaths of critical or justice-oriented work can be ruled out without ever being debated.

Amplification is the main tool used by those with power. What Apple’s analysis lacked was a structured understanding of elitist membership networks in fields controlling knowledge. In his defense, you won’t easily find an answer examining who has the power to define what teaching is for. Corporations placing members in positions of power and influence is the clearest example of direct macro level change in shaping what teaching is for. The traditional content-first approach can benefit anyone with the power to define what constitutes ‘legitimate’ content. Because curriculum is so fragmented, a modern monopoly over knowledge constitutes many nodes working together.

The content-first approach is only a means to an end, the end being a continuation of a corporate economy where wealth is determined by meeting someone else’s objectives. The end itself is a means, a means to stay in control, a means to stay in power. Amplification of aligned knowledge, rather than suppressing opposing forms of knowledge, is a much more optimized process. Dewey was the most respected name in the field when the GEB took his name, but not his work – even though Dewey worked as a professor down the hall from the newly designed Lincoln school. Ralph Tyler designed the architecture for the cycle, so the GEB lobbied for legislation using his name. Pinar and Freire spoke out against the system and weren’t silenced; they just remained in college lecture halls and not in K-12 instruction.

Seen this way, the right does not simply block change; it organizes it. Conservative modernization uses schools as a tool to reshape common sense and identity, not just policy. As Apple notes, one of its core accomplishments is to “alter the meanings of the most basic categories” we use to understand ourselves.[21] “Good schooling” becomes synonymous with high scores on standardized measures of narrow content. “Democracy” is emptied of its political struggle and remade as an economic concept organized around competition and choice.[22] The result is a system where even progressive-sounding reforms are often forced to justify themselves in conservative terms: raising test scores, increasing workforce readiness, closing “achievement gaps” so students can compete more effectively in the same unequal market.

His point is not just that conservatives have won some policy battles. It is that they currently control the language and infrastructure through which large-scale educational change is allowed to travel. If you want a new curriculum to move beyond one classroom or one school, you almost always have to route it through their anchors -  markets, standards, God, and the existing distribution of inequality. You design your unit so it “aligns to state standards.” You frame your culturally responsive lessons as ways to boost reading scores. You argue that anti-racist work will make students more employable in a diverse economy. In doing so, you use conservative modernization as a tool, even when you are trying to push against its purposes.

If conservative forces currently shape the terms of acceptable change, then progressive educators are left with a constrained set of choices. They can ignore the dominant system and work only in local, often fragile pockets. They can try to bend conservative tools toward more just ends, speaking the language of markets and standards while smuggling in different purposes. Or they can attempt to build forms of change that refuse those anchors altogether -  an option that Apple suggests is necessary but far from easy, given how deeply conservative modernization has seeped into our shared common sense.

The next section takes up that problem directly. If the right uses schools as a top-down tool for directing collective change, what kinds of change are left (literally and politically) for projects like culturally relevant education, culturally responsive pedagogy, and anti-racist curricula? How do those approaches operate when they are treated as radical, less influential, and often out of step with the official categories that conservative modernization has already locked into place? Those questions set the stage for shifting from who controls change to how forceful, bottom-up forms of change try to push back, and later, to a deeper discussion of oppression and anti-oppression as concepts rather than just tools in a policy fight.

Progressive approaches to curriculum operate very differently from the conservative mechanisms Apple describes. While conservative modernization works through state standards, policy mandates, and top-down levers of control, progressive change tends to grow from the bottom up — classrooms, communities, and the lived experiences of students. Inequality, not efficiency, is the main barrier progressives are trying to address. That focus shapes their theory of change: if the roots of inequality live in everyday experiences, then change has to start there. The challenge is that these bottom-up efforts still unfold inside a system whose categories, metrics, and priorities progressives did not create.

A good example of this tension comes from the concept of equality itself. Neither Culturally Responsive Pedagogy[23] nor Critical Pedagogy[24] lays out a clear definition of what equality actually is, or what it would mean to “reach” it. These traditions focus on justice, critical consciousness, redistribution, and liberation; not equality as a final destination, nor a stable, measurable endpoint. That ambiguity is intentional, but it also makes it harder for progressive work to scale. In a system shaped by conservative modernization and corporate assessment metrics, improvement must look like something you can measure. So when a vision refuses to define its end-goal in measurable terms, it struggles to gain traction within the structures that demand exactly that.

This comes through clearly in one of the most recognizable progressive strategies: representation. A large portion of practical CRE and CRP work revolves around questions like: Whose voices show up? Whose perspectives are centered? How much of the curriculum reflects the students sitting in front of us? Tools like the Culturally Responsive-Sustaining Education (CRSE) scorecard[25] are intentionally designed for this kind of evaluation. They help parents, teachers, and students identify where curricula exclude certain communities or reinforce dominant norms. In theory, this is a democratizing move. It invites the people closest to the learning environment to assess the curriculum themselves.

But representation as a reform strategy also carries a built-in limitation. It asks families and educators to locate inequity within a set of materials that were already built around the categories the dominant system considers important. When the scorecard asks parents to examine whether “female characters are substituted for male characters” (CRSE, 2020), it unintentionally reinforces the very binary categories it hopes to disrupt. It encourages evaluators to look for differences through the identity labels the system already recognizes: male/female, white/non-white, dominant/marginalized. Instead of destabilizing these categories, the tool has to use them to prove they’re limiting.

This isn’t a critique of the scorecard itself, it’s a reflection of the landscape progressives are forced to operate in. Conservative modernization invites certain kinds of change, but only when that change ultimately keeps the existing structure intact. In Apple’s terms, conservatives “reform” to preserve: they accept new policies, new language, even new forms of accountability, so long as the underlying logic of standardization, competition, and hierarchy remains untouched.

Progressives don’t have that luxury. Their reforms aim to disrupt the logic itself, but the tools available to them are built inside the system they’re trying to challenge. In practice, that means progressive change often ends up using the same categories, evaluative frameworks, and measurement tools that created the problem in the first place. It becomes an attempt to fix broken logic with more of the same broken logic — not because the ideas are flawed, but because the system forces them to speak in its terms in order to be seen as “credible” or “legitimate.” These are the scaffolds on a crooked tower.

Anti-racist pedagogy and culturally responsive teaching are intentionally expansive. They push toward fluidity, complexity, and identities that are always in motion. But the structures they’re working within were built during the rise of the yeoman farmer, forged in the Industrial Age, and now refined in the Corporate Era — an era defined by efficiency, categorization, and measurement. Those habits didn’t disappear. Schools still inherit a logic that sorts, labels, and compares. It’s built to make differences legible, because legibility is what the system knows how to quantify.

This is one of the main reasons anti-racist pedagogy often falls short of its potential at scale. The ideas aren’t weak; the system is rigid. It reframes broad concepts of identity as boxes to check. It treats representation as an output rather than a relationship. In trying to repair the curriculum, progressive tools end up relying on the same categories of difference that the dominant system relies on — categories shaped by corporate-era notions of efficiency and evaluation.

This becomes a structural paradox: bottom-up change has to become visible to the top before it can grow. But the moment it becomes visible, it becomes limited. In the progressive view, change is relational, iterative, and built through shared experience. Inequality remains the biggest obstacle, and addressing it requires tools that push against rigidity. Yet because conservative modernization defines the official channels of “valid” change, progressives often have to use those same channels to justify their work. Their reforms can be powerful, but their power is always partially reshaped by the system that receives it.

so-what-power.text: Educational change has never belonged to one group, one theorist, or one political camp. Change moves through a complicated chain of influence: society, theorists, institutions, politics, classrooms. Every link in that chain shapes the others. Dewey responded to the Progressive Era, Tyler codified the logic of the Corporate Era, and Apple diagnosed how conservative modernization now sets the boundaries of large-scale reform. Each of them reveals the same pattern: society shifts first, and curriculum follows. But curriculum also pushes back, often reframing the very social forces that helped produce it.

Together, these stories make one thing clear: there is no single architect of curricular change. There is instead a constant push and pull between society and schools; between theory and practice; between the foundations of the past, demands of the present, and the possibilities of the future. Sometimes conservative forces steer the channels through which official change is allowed to flow. Sometimes progressive energy disrupts those channels from below. But neither side determines everything. Curriculum lives in the tension between the two.
If we misunderstand who moves change, we will misunderstand how to move it ourselves.

I hope you do not confuse this chapter as labeling curriculum as political, but that political dominance is just one major factor which shapes society. In a way, we are all responsible for change in curriculum. Theorists have their role to play; educators have theirs. Those logics act as the “middle man” between theory and practice. Unless we see how those forces interact, how they reinforce, distort, resist, or redirect one another, we cannot design a curriculum that is capable of doing anything more than repeating the patterns of its moment.

Curriculum reform so often fails to live up to its promises. Not because theorists lack vision, or because teachers lack skill, but because change is always filtered through structures and assumptions inherited from earlier periods. If Dewey struggled in the Industrial Age and Tyler was reshaped by the Corporate Age, it should not surprise us that today’s justice-oriented work is contending with the deeply embedded logic of conservative modernization. This positions us to imagine a curriculum that does not simply react to the forces around it, but actively reshapes how those forces are understood.

who-no-power.text: If society is what changes curriculum, what changes society? We discussed the higher level battels of the conservative maintenance, and even zoomed in on the progressive identity aspect, now lets go a little deeper. The values and experiences of the people in a society collectively form the values of the society. Those in power in a society manipulate those values and control the societal narrative. It’s natural that the dominant culture tends to lean conservative, whereas those under oppression tend to be the ones fighting for change. The goal of any equitable system is to avoid structure around a dominant norm; for there simply to be no dominant norm.

who-oppressed.text: [when revising: this section needs to present the traditionally oppressed groups as the object in sentences and paragraphs, not the subject. I want to express how the dominant culture is oppressed by their own realities as well as the races that those dominant cultures suppressed (so it’s ok to have the dominant culture as the object when discussing their

Historically, the United States has had a unique relationship with hegemony compared to other nations. At a time where centuries old empires controlled the world, the United States rebelled against the idea of nationhood. Instead of a nation founded on a race, religion, language, myth, or conquest, rugged Americans came together, fought together, and died together in the dream of a free republic. The United States was formed on a belief, a skewed interpretation by today’s standards, but a noble effort nonetheless: all men are created equal. The role of government, despite ideological debates surrounding its power and influence, was largely agreed by the Framers to be the protector of individual rights of man.

Many historians debate the ending of the revolution; “when did it end?” “did it end?” or more existentially, “can it ever end?” These debates are more philosophical in nature, but they incite interesting discussions. Equality, to the Framers, meant white propertied men. To Andrew Jackson in 1830, it meant all white men. To Susan B. Anthony and Elizebeth Cady Stanton, it meant white men and women. To Abigail Adams, it meant all men and women. Frederick Douglass, MLK Jr., Malcom X., Wong Kim Ark, Fred Korematzu, and Sitting Bull all view equality differently and independently.

Because true equality is a utopia individually held, unable to be realized, part of progression is recognizing that there will ultimately be a dominant prevailing set of norms in society. These dominant set of norms can exist in a tremendous number of forms including hidden/null curriculum, systemic racism, heterosexual normativity, political allegiance, religion, and an infinite amount of others. A member of a society is inherently oppressed by dominant mannerisms and beliefs of right and wrong, good and bad. Schools provide a unique control group for examining oppression as grouping naturally occurs on every level – from the seating arrangement at a lunch table to funding distributions in a locality or state.

Kevin Kumashiro addresses oppression in education twofold: “The first approach to addressing oppression focuses on improving the experiences of students who are Othered or in some way oppressed in and by mainstream society… [and] by looking at assumptions about and expectations for the Other—especially those held by educators—that influence how the Other is treated.”[26] It is multiple, situated, and produced through both external treatment and internal ways of knowing, but also through structural forces, ideologies, and discursive repetition.

He goes on to break “oppression” into different categories, specifically in how to recognize it in educational contexts. Oppression as external harm is the “recognizable’’ oppression: differential treatment based on race, gender, sexuality, or class. This can be in the form(s) of harassment, exclusion, violence, deliberate lack of resources, intentional neglect, or unequal attention.

Oppression also arises from the beliefs educators carry about who students are or should be. Often referred to as the “hidden curriculum,” Oppression as Internal Dispositions and Assumptions produces harm even if no overt bad behavior occurs, often through racial stereotypes, sexist assumptions, heterosexual expectations, or assimilationist beliefs. Strictly speaking, by all known conception, it is impossible to teach the entirety of all knowledge in any subject, field, ensuring the unavoidability of the hidden curriculum.[27]

While he does note the nuance in many parts, Kumashiro orbits his entire framework around his assumption of “who” is oppressed directly, crafting his definitions of oppression around identifiable characteristics. In the first section, he defines ‘Otherness’ by first identifying the dominant norm, then identify everyone who differs from it. The examples he lists stem from the dominant group, "the majority of students—namely, all those who are not White American, male, hegemonically masculine, heterosexual, and middle-class or wealthy... other traditionally marginalized groups, such as students with disabilities, students with limited or no English-language proficiency, and students from non-Christian religious backgrounds.” Anyone who deviates from this even slightly is then classified as an “Other.”

Kevin Kumashiro’s work is certainly profound despite my redacted, heavy critique on his classification. It is true in many cases that each of those identifiers carry a perception of dominance and in many cases have benefited in some way due to one or more of those identifiers. The issue comes with the analysis of the ‘Other.’ If the aim of anti-racist pedagogy is to reduce racism on the personal, educational, or system level, then perhaps it would be wise to identify solutions that don’t depend on an investigation into race. Would it be wrong to shift the focus over to generalized oppression rather than narrowly focus on specific groups?

a-place-in-time.text: Many, including myself, argue that the American Revolution did not end in 1783. It continues to be tested and weathered. The distant echoes of liberty sing through the generations. The fight of the suffragettes, abolitionists, and reformers lives on in all of us. Regardless of one’s point of view towards race, sex, or sexuality, it is difficult to argue the expansion of WE the people. Let’s now analyze the structures and frameworks which guided enlightened equality in the 18th century.[28]

reality-of-race.text: What was anti-racist before anti-racism? History of anti-racism?

[EDIT – MAKE SURE TO INTORDUCE RACE HERE AS A MUCH MORE MULTIFASCETED CONCEPT THAN JUST BLACK VS WHITE, AND TRANSITION THAT INTO WHY I’M NARROWING IT DOWN TO BLACK VS WHITE – there needs to be a reason (it’s because it’s the most well-documented account of objective racial standings and societal hierarchies) ---   the whole point of me breaking it down this structurally is to demonstrate how it fails. How my analysis on these two races don’t account for the different races, ethnicities, nuances within each race, overlap between racial ideologies, who gets to shape them. You can only get to those questions when you don’t confine your search to race itself.]

The early decades of racial tension culminated at Ft. Sumpter in 1861 forcing many Americans to consider their position on our “peculiar institution” whether they wanted to or not. It was the tendency of those in power to suppress their own thinking of the matter; it was easier to put it off than address it head on. In fact, that’s exactly what the Framers did. Rather than ending the slave trade in 1789, they wrote it into the Constitution to be revisited in 20 years. Decades piled on top of each other as compromises were made and deals were struck – all without the realization and acceptance that an attribute does not inherently determine worth.

More importantly, decisions were made without the consideration of the ‘Other.’ Why did all three branches of government relinquish their protection of individual rights when the color of one’s skin was different to their own? Some early Americans prided the diversity of the Scotts, Irish, Dutch, German, British, French, and Indian cohabitation and mingling. The Frontier was populated by intermingling groups and nationalities. Yet the ideas of race differed among individuals and colonies. People from Africa were hardly ever seen as equal by many; different experiences of Europeans and Indians caused varying identity relationships.

Racial tensions in most discourse focused heavily on white and black relations. Census data from 1860 recorded an estimated 3.94 million enslaved people, yet slaveowners to be just 10% of that. On many plantations, there were upwards of 100 slaves. On one plantation in Georgetown, South Carolina, 1,092 people were written off to be slaves of a single man. With this dominance of enslaved people, one may be left wondering why attempts at slave revolts failed.

In 1800, an enslaved Virginian, Gabriel, attempted to abolish slavery by seizing control of the state capitol and holding hostages as ransom – including the governor and future president of the United States, James Monroe. Gabriel’s rebellion failed for two main reasons: weather and informants. A score and two years later, inspiration of the Haitian Revolution gave motivation to another ‘radical’[29] rebellion led by an enslaved South Carolinian named Denmark Vessey. Unfortunately for Vessey and the 131 others arrested in the process, yet another slave revolt was foiled by informants.

These acts of rebellion demonstrate the reality for many living in the time, not necessarily because of their fight towards practical equality, but because of their battle against the very reality itself. In both presented examples, the informants who reported these activities were not freemen, not plantation owners, but other slaves themselves. For most free and enslaved Americans alike in the early republic, extreme oppression was not merely a way of life – it was a reality. Enslaved and other suppressed Americans had no say over their own identity, it was assigned to them by another group.

Anti-racism and equality of the time was ironically less fragmented than it is today; still just as nuanced, but mainstream ideologies surrounding identity were on a different spectrum than one to even be considered today. In a linear view, anti-racist theorists today may look at our current climate and realize that we have made definitive progress despite sustaining oppression. However, tracing this fight linearly presents three fundamental issues:
It assumes the morality and standards of one’s time are closer to a universal, fundamental truth or end goal of anti-racism;
Often times equality is viewed as a dichotomy between two or more specific groups without accounting for the nuance and spectrums of each member; and more dangerously,
Modern anti-racist practices assume that the oppressors themselves cannot be oppressed.
Two examples help prove the limitation of these mindsets: the relationship between Frederick Douglass and Abraham Lincoln, and the infamous doll test of Brown v. Board of Education.

In his first meeting with the Great Emancipator, Frederick Douglass felt disregarded, and frankly disappointed, by Lincoln’s abolitionist philosophy. Abolitionism and anti-racism were competingly aligned attitudes towards an issue with differing levels of importance. Not all abolitionists viewed enslaved Americans as equals. Lincoln himself proposed that emancipated Americans be deported to Liberia; at another point he suggested finding them a home in Latin America. During the infamous senatorial campaign debates just two years before being elected as President, he states explicitly “I am not, nor ever have been, in favor of bringing about in any way the social and political equality of the white and black races.”

The self-emancipated slave had a different attitude towards oppression and fighting it. His struggles and discontentment were based on a much more rigid set of factors in which the dominant society was not only ignoring the voices of the oppressed, the consideration of the consideration itself was not possible. Like the enslaved informants in 1800 and 1822 who would rather face the confines of slavery than a reality beyond their ability to comprehend, many in the sphere of dominance did not have the ability to explore the concept of true equality.

This made it especially difficult for change to happen in a confined world limited to the realities of society. The determination and resilience of Frederick Douglass’ past allowed him to engage in productive conversations with one of the major shapers of zeitgeistian societal realities – President Lincoln. The accomplishments of Douglass may have seemed more impressive to an enslaved person than the accomplishments of Lincoln’s rise to presidency by a free Illinoisian.

Douglass’s own views on race and anti-racism also developed during his life. With each new phase of his life, new possibilities opened and the ability to start seeing new, hazy realities emerged. In later reflections in Narrative (1845), Douglass writes that his early years confined to the limited scope of his enslavement made it difficult to imagine freedom for all enslaved. His focus was determined on proving his “humanity” in terms white abolitionists already accepted. Once breaking his chains, Douglass rapidly shifted to a more global adherence to abolitionism, one centered around equality. This was different than the dominant “ending slavery” interpretation of abolition which did not acknowledge the equality of races. His evolution in his attitudes and theories towards race not only document the growth of his racial framework, but also shine light on the global evolution happening on the societal level.

Admittedly, Lincoln also experienced an evolution in his thinking and attitudes toward race over the course of his life. Just a year before his death, Lincoln reflects on these aspects. In a letter to a confederate veteran, he humbly acknowledges: “I claim not to have controlled events, but confess plainly that events have controlled me.”

After their first meeting in 1863, Douglass wrote that he was “not satisfied with him” and his slow efforts at abolition. He also argued Lincoln’s humility in the face of his role was a weakness rather than a strength: “He argued like an attorney, I wanted him to act like a commander-in-chief.” Lincoln invited Douglass back in 1864 to get his opinion on certain aspects of the Civil War and emancipation. This surprised Douglass even though the strategies and opinions were not necessarily taken into account.

Lincoln’s role as president certainly made him unique, and he recognized that. His humility of his role is ranked by historians as one of his more admirable qualities. The nation, in his mind, chose him to lead. He also recognized that a major influential factor for voters was the issue of race and slavery. The nation who chose him to lead was divided. Even with only garnering 39% of the popular vote, 1,855,276 individual votes were cast in his name. Was he only supposed to lead them? What about the 2,267,623 people who voted against him? Should they have a voice? What about those who could not even vote; those who were a cornerstone for ideological divide; those whose back the economy rested on; those who many in America still regarded as ‘property’ and not human? The 1860 census data reported 3,953,760 Americans to be enslaved –5% less than the total number of Americans who casted a vote.

Is it reasonable to expect a single man from the frontier, who has traveled little in his time, to represent the ideas, interests, and experiences of all Americans? Lincoln, like everyone else, was a product of his own experiences. He was, in a sense, oppressed by his beliefs and situation. Depression played a major role in the middle of Lincoln’s life. During a period of severe depression, suicide intervention became necessary. Some historians today theorize that a possibly shamed and suppressed sexuality left unexplored contributed to his mental health.

Both Douglass and Lincoln share many similarities and differences. Is it the blackness or whiteness that causes these? Social Darwinism may support that; however, the complexity and nuance of race shows that it is the societal ideas surrounding race that causes similarities and differences. The evolution, grounding, contextualization, perspectives, and experiences – all shaping factors of racial identity and attitudes according to modern anti-racist theorists today – continue to grow, shrink, and even expand to new axes.

Following the Civil War and the dissipation of race-based slavery, that limitedly explored societal reality of race was expanded. Even those who vehemently disagreed with abolition, those who previously did not have opportunities (and in turn, capabilities) to consider slaves as anything other than property, were introduced to new possibility that the person they ‘bought’ might actually be a person. On another end of the spectrum, the person who was born into slavery had a vastly different perspective on the idea of human rights. These examples are of course major oversimplifications of the nuances and constructs that exist(ed), but the focus on the extreme hopefully allows opportunity to explore in middle grounds and potentially other realities.

group-ideology.text: The emergence of dominant post-war anti-racism evolved from the societal conceptions grown from the collective experiences of individuals. Since the beginning of civilization, the possibility of conquest and power has been dependent on variations of slavery and prejudice. Perhaps it is natural for homo sapiens to feel a bond in a group. Even before civilization, before agriculture, and even before what many agree to be the emergence of consciousness, it is theorized that we genocided our last other sibling species. Yuval Noah Hurrarih, meta-historian and anthropologist, additionally draws attention to the genocide and extinction of hundreds of species of large animals, nearly depopulating continents in the process.[30]

The ideology surrounding group-based thinking confines individuality to a collective middle ground which often times does not encapsulate the nuance and perspectives of those individual perspectives. When one group becomes dominant, the assumption of its purpose becomes what the majority of others agree to be the assumption. This can be done through many forms and has been discussed and debated for the entirety of philosophy; however, it is the societal acceptance of the group’s attributes by society that determines its validity.

When analyzing group-based identity, it is of course required that there be an identifiable group to be analyzed.[31] Any grouping of people today can only be possible because of the groupings of yesterday, consisting of no two people with a consensus on the group’s purpose and identity. This alone makes it nearly impossible to analyze a group. Yet, society and exploration are dependent on collaboration and, in turn, grouping. The aim is not to analyze grouping by a confinement of identifiable collections of characteristics, but rather analyze the components themselves.

In analyzing racial groupings for instance, the analyzation becomes confined by the structures of race itself. While the intentions of racist and anti-racist theories intend to serve opposite practices, the approaches share many similarities. Both examine race by considering it as the denominator of the equation rather than a variable. In classic math, reducing a denominator to 0 breaks math itself. Because of this logic, race must remain the underlying cause and cannot be removed from the equation.

For racial theory, especially social-Darwanistic theory, race is inherent to natural groupings, and in many cases, it acts as the justification for continued racial oppression. For these theorists, racial oppression may be viewed as the systems that nature produced. In turn, race is the common denominator.

Anti-racists center their approaches on combatting racism through identifying it. In simple, any defense or critique about racially led thinking is supported by evidence which is then tied to race. Unveiling the “hidden curriculum” of society is impossible without drawing attention to the curtain itself. Anti-racial pedagogy cannot be discussed without identifying issues in racial relations to begin with. The identification aspect relies on relating examples of oppression to ideas of race. However, since race is a societal concept that should have as little determination on ones perception by others as the color of one’s hair, is it best to continue to point out the differences (or similarities) of race?

Experiments conducted in the 1940’s, and antiquated “separate but equal” policies in education, demonstrated the effects of race-centered societal narratives. To demonstrate the psychological factors at play in shaping a child’s identity, Kenneth and Mamie Clark asked children to choose which adjectives and attributes belonged to a white or black doll. Unsurprisingly to the researchers, white students tended to prefer the white dolls and associate negative attributes, like “looks bad,” to the black dolls. It was the reaction of black students that made the argument for separation being unequal (“The Doll Study”).

This evidence alone is not just another depiction of societal reality to the respondents; it identifies what Clark and Clark call a “fundamental conflict” of the ego.[32] Northern integrated schools showed a higher sense of evasiveness and anxiety towards race in black participants. Clark and Clark go on to say that “Northern children refused to continue in the experiment when they were confronted with the task of identifying with a brown-skin color after they had already negated the brown and indicated a preference for white.”[33]

The authors conclude that while Southern children could matter-of-factly state that the brown doll was "ugly" because they accepted the racial hierarchy they lived in, Northern children were in a state of emotional conflict. They knew they weren't supposed to be inferior (or perhaps knew it was a sensitive topic), yet they still felt inferior. This conflict between their reality and their feelings caused them to "repress," "escape," and "refuse to continue."

This study confirmed common beliefs of the time; its goal was not to create the theory but further prove it. The impact of the results led to the de facto end of segregation in public spaces in the United States for the first time in its history; however, the issue of race was not finished. In fact, it began to take new light. Societal attempts to deal with race increased the very evasiveness that integrated schools promoted. Researchers and psychologists believed that success metrics in racist ideologies could be assessed by similar doll tests – many have been rebuilt since. The goals of which were always presenting students with attributes and sentiments based solely on race to determine if there was societal prejudice against color alone.

While the merits of the doll test certainly proved success in the anti-racist community, it maintains the view of race as a legitimate concept as opposed to a societally structured one. Schools today that subscribe to anti-racist pedagogical efforts invite students, parents, and teachers to consistently assess race across all metrics. Curriculum evaluations like EdReports and the CRE Scorecard include indicators for parents to ensure student materials put “non-White or female characters in the place of White male characters.”[34]

A parent reading this is left largely on their own for defining a non-white character. Because of societal definitions of race, there is a collective understanding that most Americans would be able to define. When the participants in the Doll Study were asked which color they’d use to draw a person they wished to be, the “non-evasive” students in large amount chose the white or yellow crayon. They intrinsically knew which race was “better” because they were told how to think. The direct impacts on the systemic definitions of race were engrained again and again. Even students from integrated northern schools chose to avoid the topic.

Put yourself in the position of a student’s parent today. Caring about their education, you decide to evaluate their materials to ensure it meets the quality of your standards. A simple Google search or ChatGPT request brings you to the CRE Scorecard which you decide to use.  You begin to examine the 8th grade ELA curriculum and see the required reading lists How to Kill a Mockingbird – a controversial book in today’s climate. The setting being in the deep south during the Great Depression presents a narrow lens which the author allows himself to explore.

How do you, as a parent, begin analyzing racial attitudes? Even with the stereotypes and other collective agreements of differences between race, individuals all have different interpretations of the broader aspects. For example, will a black parent look for the same stereotypes as a white parent? Will an Asian parent view racial stereotypes the same as even another Asian parent? In order to complete this scorecard, you must give a quantifiable response towards the representation of stereotypical behaviors – which means you must first think of and define what a stereotypical behavior of a race is.

In an attempt to distance yourself from race being a barrier, anti-racists believe the best way to break down race is by confronting it. I am not suggesting race shouldn’t be confronted, nor am I suggesting race does not play a role in individuals lives; I’m in fact saying the opposite. The ideas and attitudes towards and surround racial tendencies are a subconscious factor of how every individual views the world. By defining a stereotype, even with the intention of confronting and collapsing it, one is reinforcing the viewed differences between race.

The progressive achievements of anti-racist pedagogy should not be understated. Though the ideas behind anti-racist theory have dramatically changed, the progression towards an equality of races has trended successfully. Integrations of schools allowed realities of equality to form throughout the different localities of the United States. Quotas, DEI, and anti-racist pedagogy have allowed for a higher percentage of non-white individuals in dominant positions of society. However, the continuation of associating attributes with identity proves more deceive than equal.

This section intentionally kept a narrow lens of race between black and white. Of course, there are many other races who face both similar and different forms of oppression of which I omitted for much of this. Mixed race children, or children adopted by parents of different races have noted feelings of displacement – not knowing which race to feel. To some, this may come across as radical, revolutionary, or immoral; to others, obvious or not far enough: it is not possible for there to be racism, sexism, homophobia, or other intentional marginalization of group at the individual level of society.[35] All of these labeling, groupings, and segregation is an entirely societal concept. This is not meant to imply that ‘othering’ can’t be done on an individualistic level – it certainly can. Every action or thought, in a way, is inspired by society’s impression of one’s race.

But our ideas will change and evolve, as they have with every generation. The concept of oppression has expanded drastically just in the last 250 years. Early dominant discourse rarely engaged in conversation of sexuality, transgenderism, or even wealth. Today, we are witnessing the birth of artificial thought. Will our children condemn our slavery of LLM’s? Will their children fault a grocery shopper who buys chicken off the shelf? Harrari notes that if just 10% of animal rights exist, as defined by “extreme” activists, our chicken harvesting industries are the greatest acts of cruelty by our species.

cognitive-oppression.text: Analyzing sequences rather than individual points provides more overall insight. One cannot oppress oneself, another, nor be oppressed by one’s environment/society. With only a single consciousness, a single ability to conceive meaning, all acts in the society are equalized. When a society scales, archeologists and historians agree that the size of such society wildly and drastically shift in terms of economic, political, militaristic, intellectualistic… capabilities. Modes and abilities of oppression are therefore undoubtably different when examining case studies at different levels. Internalized oppression is an unavoidable reality of the human consciousness. The only cure to internalized oppression is the loss of consciousness (the ability to make meaning) or to be omniscient and omnipotent (aka the ability to make meaning out of every conceivable understanding of every possible reality). When a student learns a new concept (creating meaning by fluxion), their comprehension is limited by that which they already have learnt. Depending on one’s ability to interpret oppression, they may be inclined to attribute positive and negative feelings towards various effects of internalized oppression. A student more concerned about time dedicated to TikTok than experimenting in science, may value an extreme amount of internalized oppression. Limited ability to explore, question, wonder, and think creates a cognitive environment free from responsibility.

As a concept, internalized oppression is possible to combat. illusion-diff.text: Despite surface differences such as funding or location, the foundational architecture of American public schooling is identical: age-graded cohorts, bell schedules, and the revolutions around the “Core Four” subjects. Nearly every elementary student is encouraged to learn basic math and how to read. In middle school, students are introduced to essay writing and scientific method. In high school, almost any student pursuing a higher education takes the SAT, ACT, AP/IB courses, or some other form of standardized test in order to be compared against thousands of others for college admissions.

Debates rage across party, region, and religion as to what content should or shouldn’t be taught. Often times a product of grouping mentality, parents, students, or community members may assume active roles in the shaping of education or curriculum adoption. This is done in many ways, including board meetings, self/peer evaluations, or through contact with their child or child’s teachers/administrators. many cases, public schools have been forced to remove books, alter course content, or make structural changes. But these battles are often distractions; the debates remain endless and cyclical – there will always be aspects of the main, null, or hidden curriculum that promote oppression.

Due to the collective structure of assessment and evaluation of curriculum and of students, change tends to affect more than just the student asking for it. For instance, a parent demanding his daughter learns about the Rwandan Genocide for more than a brief mention in her world history class would imply the teacher modify her curriculum for the entire class. Perhaps they can offer more of a variety in terms of assignments given during that unit – but with objectives and state standards to assess for, alignment of multiple assignments might be difficult.

More tellingly, methods of differentiated learning increasingly rely on accommodations such as IEPs and 504s. The system attempts to scaffold students with 'learning disabilities' by assuming that any deviation from the dominant average is a deficit. But this reveals a structural flaw: Why does the 'regular' classroom require legal documentation to accommodate natural human variation? Again and again, the assumptions of a 'right' way to learn limit the opportunities for metacognition. It assumes that 'normal' learners are identical, and that those with different cognitive topologies must be retrofitted to the standard model.

A deaf or blind student would have tremendous difficulty passing assessments in the average US public school. Is there a physical internal difference in the capacity to think between someone who is deaf and someone who is not? Not necessarily. Aside from hearing, the barrier is not the math or the literature but the prescribed architecture of delivery and deterministic standardized assessments. We don’t need a system that accommodates exceptions; we need a system where cognitive variation is the assumption.

Assumptions about a "correct" schooling model prevent learners with physical or cognitive variabilities from success without segregation or accommodation. In a content-first curriculum, the implication of a "right" and "wrong" mentality oppresses perspective into a dichromatic lens. It challenges us to look for a middle ground, but  there is no single, fixed middle ground everyone can occupy; there are only overlapping, shifting shared understandings that must be consciously negotiated.

If experiences form the interconnected nodes of awareness, then the cognitive perception of an idea cannot be equally shared between two people. Therefore, the role of school is not to force students to meet in the middle, but to teach them how to bridge the gap, how to consciously update one’s reality autonomously – to learn how to learn.

communication.text: If learning is about bridging realities rather than forcing everyone to meet in the middle, then communication becomes the key commodity in translating an idea or a thought from one’s own consciousness into one of the infinite modes of articulated expression. Traditionally, communication is measured in structured, often binary ways such as multiple-choice questions, essay rubrics, or an answer key. Because of objective and standard alignment, assessment differentiation can easily become inequitable. A teacher who allows assessment options to be submitted as an essay, podcast, or poem must create different ways of measuring a student’s ability to communicate achievement of an objective – often through communicating knowledge.

Every interaction consists of many forms of communication. Even without intentional effort, bodies are constantly ‘communicating’ with themselves through automatic processes. With little to no conscious consumption, one’s body communicates with it to pump the heart, breathe, or blink. More commonly observed as communication, actions such as reading, writing, or speaking are forms of external communication. Intentional and unintentional facial expressions, systematic body language, or other “tells” can communicate subconscious emotion or thought. Metacognition itself is a form of internal communication.

In specific professional fields, strictly structured communication is not just preferable, it can be necessary. Collective agreements around “truths” provide emergency life-saving precision in surgery rooms. For a non-surgeon, the difference between a hemostat and a needle holder may mean nothing. But if a surgeon called for a hemostat to clamp a vessel and the scrub tech handed over the needle holder, the aggressive jaws could crush and macerate the delicate blood vessel, potentially causing more bleeding rather than stopping it.

The problem is not that strict codes exist, or even that structure, precision, and accuracy are core components of academic access. The reliance on memorization and correct answers as the only metric is what hinders metacognition. Schools become confused with operating rooms where scrub techs are assessed on accuracy under pressure. However, a patient’s surgery is equally dependent on the scrub tech’s ability to recognize a hemostat from a needle holder and the surgeons understanding of where, how, and why to use what tools when. We confuse the memorization of the tool (the hemostat) with the judgment required to use it.

Chemists, musicians, and bakers all communicate success in seemingly different ways. A chemist articulates success by publishing lab results in a peer-reviewed journal documenting her experiment’s hypothesis, results, and analysis. A musician has a different type of flexibility in terms of communicating alignment toward an objective. The variation of communication style is displayed in how a piece is played, sung, composed, or arranged. Musicians can communicate their perspectives and individual, autonomous distinctiveness by taking liberties in aspects of rhythm, pitch, transposition, remix, or covers. Much like snowflakes, a song cannot possibly be played the same way live twice. The timing, hertz frequencies, and many other tiny variables make it so that even the most consistent musician can never exactly recommunicate their reality. These differences become even clearer when both are asked to follow the same “recipe” in a space like a baking contest.

Both the chemist and musician might go about communication in a very different way. A chemist, whose day-to-day work consists largely of precise measurements and expected chemical-reaction outcomes, would be more likely to stick to a strict interpretation of the recipe, attempting little variation. The musician, whose life consists of a more abstract form of communication, may take more liberties by adding their own flair to the recipe. In a metacognitive curriculum, these varied modes of communication are not just outputs to be graded, but starting points for students to notice, name, and refine how they learn.

Just as disciplines differ in how they communicate success, school subjects are not as cleanly separated as their schedules suggest. A student in a high school biology class might think that his history class shares no overlap with his lab assignment on hierarchies and the classification of organisms. History class, meanwhile, covers the great ancient empires of the old world. The student will go from his lab to his lecture on the collapse of the Roman Republic and patrician off the knowledge from biology. There is no inherent opportunity, invitation, nor incentivization for the student to draw connections between the two fields.[37]

Biology and history both invite learners to see and question hierarchies, whether in the classification of organisms or in the structuring of societies and empires. Chemistry’s themes of cause, effect, and reaction parallel historical chains of action and consequence. When we limit content to tightly bounded subject silos, we implicitly teach that each discipline’s way of thinking and communicating is fixed. That is a static cognition belief, not a metacognitive habit.

metacognition.text: Most communication is subtle, unintentional, or quickly forgotten. Not many people are blessed, or cursed, with a perfect photographic memory. Remembering your last conversation exactly word for word is nearly impossible and not often attempted. However, you might remember the topic of the conversation, emotions you felt during it, or a task or takeaway. After a time, subtle cues and unintentional modes of communication during the conversation become as blended together as the actual verbatim words. Metacognition is what lets us step back from those blended impressions and ask how we made sense of them, why we reacted the way we did, and how our patterns of thinking might change next time.

Cognition is innate and inherent for homo sapiens. Life’s unique gift of awareness conducted by memory allows for cognition’s existence. Interpreting literary text by the words rather than the theme, engaging in a conversation without focusing on anything aside from the exchanging of words, or solving 2 + 2, are all forms of cognition. It is the ability to realize, understand, and recall memories and knowledge. Metacognition adds another layer: it is the ability to notice and shape one’s own thinking – to understand how ideas, thoughts, and abstract concepts connect to everything else, and to decide how to navigate those connections. It’s the ability to see the lines connecting the various nodes in one’s awareness and to adjust navigation along those lines.

Over the past few decades, metacognition has generally been defined as people’s knowledge of and control over their own thinking. Introducing the term to pedagogical research, J.H. Flavell describes metacognition as “knowledge and cognition about cognitive phenomena,” or in other words, cognitions about one’s own cognitions.[38] Schraw and Dennison build on this by distinguishing knowledge of cognition (being aware of how you think) from regulation of cognition (planning, monitoring, and evaluating how you are thinking).[39] Veenman and colleagues similarly highlight planning, monitoring, and evaluation or judgment as core metacognitive skills that influence how students approach tasks and how well they perform.[40]

Neuroscience has started to map this capacity to specific brain systems: research on decision-making suggests that regions in the anterior and rostrolateral prefrontal cortex are especially involved in monitoring confidence and accuracy, or more simply in how we “think about” our own judgments.[41] In education, meta-analyses like Hattie’s Visible Learning and later work on learning strategies consistently show that metacognitive strategies (knowing how you learn, monitoring your understanding, adjusting strategies) have a sizable positive impact on student achievement.[42] In other words, metacognition is not just a nice add-on; it is one of the main engines of effective learning.

Acknowledging the similarities and differences in the baking results between the chemist and the musician is a form of cognition. In a classroom setting with a student performing at a high level in chemistry and a student performing at a high level in orchestra, their skills and forms of communication should not necessarily be assessed the same way.[43] In society, schools included, there are a set of universal agreements, like 1.01 cups of flour being essentially the same as 1.00 cups when baking cookies. But if the musician decided to use .75 cups flour and an extra 25% of sugar, that’s a cognitively significant variation from the recipe. If the baking evaluation were based on alignment to a rubric with indicators of exact recipe usage, the musician would have points taken off and the chemist would not.

A metacognitive evaluation would not assume the musician did anything wrong; rather, it would evaluate the musician’s opportunity to learn about their own learning. Why did the student make that choice? Was it because they couldn’t read the recipe correctly? Was it because they felt the best expression of their baking communication would be a counternormative take on brownies? Perhaps it was out of deliberate curiosity to invent something new. A traditional evaluation would treat the deviation as an error; a metacognitive evaluation treats it as data. The point is not to reward or punish the choice, but to surface and refine the thinking behind it.

Of course, stakeholders at the other end of communication also matter. Much like the example with surgeons, it would be impractical to refrain from merging your reality with that of others. In an evaluation on baking for a specific type of customer, the assessment might look different. Perhaps it is an interdisciplinary experiment to construct a cake in the same style as the Framers constructing the Constitution. In that case, a decision to design a marble cake in the spirit of federalism might carry more weight than the result. In other circumstances, the chemistry of the cake might carry more weight in assessment than the artistic parameters.

What objective would you be assessing for in this case? What state standard would be achieved by this evaluation? One answer might be that you are assessing students’ understanding of how structural compromises shape both the stability and fragility of a system. But there is no neat standard labeled “experiences the ethical instability of representational injustice through baking.” That gap exposes how content-anchored objectives struggle to capture metacognitive and conceptual work that spills across disciplines.

Certain conceptual objectives are necessary to ensure metacognition is being activated and time is not spent unproductively. But these objectives should not be set in stone. They should evolve throughout the entire process of the assignment, lesson, unit, course, or educational journey. Unfortunately, these types of experiments are often considered distractions from core knowledge because they might take too much time away from other information. Another critique has been shouting through the cracks: if the dominant traditional model of curriculum is “working” for most people, and IEPs and 504s provide scaffolded support, why shift evaluation to allow for differentiated forms of communication and objectives if everyone would still have to do the same thing?

The answer is that “doing the same thing” is not the same as “learning in the same way.” A system that treats accommodations as legal exceptions to a fixed path may help more students reach the test, but it still withholds the chance to understand and redesign their own patterns of thinking. Metacognition is not an extra support layered onto a content-first curriculum; it is the work of becoming aware of and responsible for one’s own learning.

The differentiation of cognition and metacognition has been justified here. Content proves to be a major limiting factor in metacognitive exploration. Corporate-era logic, with its emphasis on fixed objectives, efficiency, and accuracy, hinders individuals from proving their worth in their strongest modes of communication. If curriculum can no longer be organized around stable content, it has to be organized around something else: the ways students learn, revise, and communicate their thinking. So if not content, then it should focus on metacognition. But what would a curriculum that supports metacognition look like? What provides solutions to the taped scaffolds of the crooked buildings?

Sequential and hierarchical structures of schooling come with major limitations (as outlined earlier),[44] yet some form of structure is unavoidable: without it, communication and assessment collapse into noise. Unstructured or poorly structured experiences were exactly what Dewey criticized in early progressive education; good intentions without productive form. So the question becomes: How do we design structures that support the monitoring side of metacognition in a controlled educational environment, rather than shutting it down?

In this book, I call those structures Contextures: interwoven learning environments that bring together themes, tasks, and sources so that students can work on how they learn, not just what they learn. A Contexture is not a “unit on the American Revolution” or a “biology class.” It is a deliberate weave of experiences through which students are invited to notice, question, and reorganize their own thinking. The point of a Contexture is Cogniscence: learning that includes awareness of how it is changing what you know and how you are able to know. When students cognesce inside a Contexture, they are not only acquiring information; they are practicing learning-how-to-learn in ways they can carry into new situations.

Throughout this book, I have been developing six metacognitive habits: Endospection, Omniperegrination, Constellaration, Refraction, Exospection, and Synthesis, as the core practices of Cogniscence. Each habit names a different way of monitoring and directing one’s thinking. Together, they define what it means in this model, to “learn how to learn.” Designing school around Contextures means designing around these habits: asking not only “What should students know?” but “Which habits are they exercising here, and how?”

Endospection is the starting point: if metacognition is about monitoring and directing one’s own thinking, we have to ask who, exactly, is doing the monitoring. I picture that “who” as a pulsing sphere of selfhood, the Endosphere: the current, always-changing configuration of who we take ourselves to be. Endospection is the habit of returning to, narrating, and revising that Endosphere over time. A curriculum that names Endospection and the Endosphere explicitly treats self-identity as an object of study rather than an invisible background condition. It matters because every other habit—Omnipere’s wandering, Constellare’s research, Refraction’s critique—rests on some sense of who is thinking, for whom, and why.
