endospection-impl.text: AMC Studios released a two-season show called Pantheon in 2022 on the topic of Uploaded Intelligence.[46] Although it’s set in a near-future version of our world, the technology it depicts is far beyond what we can currently do; the ethical questions it raises, however, are squarely aimed at our present moment. In Pantheon, advances in artificial intelligence and neurotechnology allow private corporations to scan a person’s brain, encode their memories, sensations, and personality onto hard drives, and in the process destroy their biological body. Can the self be preserved in an artificial environment without the biological components such as the brain, heart, or perhaps a separate soul?

Debates with friends and family over specific episodes showed me the range of perspectives. The conclusion I came to does not imply “correctness,” simply a justified conclusion: as long as the self is believed in, the self exists. Much like the concepts of race, sexuality, currency, or social status, the conception of the self is based on experience-formed awareness conducted by memory. There is a sense in which the self is a story we continuously tell and retell.

At the same time, self-identity, as determined by René Descartes, is the only truth beyond doubt. In his Meditations, Descartes found this kind of radical self-examination to be difficult, even frightening. When he tried to doubt the reality of everything, he brushed up against nihilism before finding an anchor in simple logic. Doubting, he realized, requires thinking; doubting that you are thinking is itself a form of thought. If thought makes doubting possible, and doubting is already a kind of thinking, then the existence of a thinking self cannot be doubted out of existence. For Descartes, the self does not depend on what you believe about the world; it is guaranteed by the very act of thinking, the cogito – I think, therefore I am.

From a contemporary perspective, this raises an uncomfortable question: when, if ever, does that thinking self actually “switch off”? Everyday life already offers liminal cases. During deep, dreamless sleep, people report no conscious experience at all, even though brain activity continues and dreaming can occur in other sleep stages. Neuroscience studies show that consciousness during sleep waxes and wanes with changes in large-scale brain activity, particularly in posterior cortical regions that support the content of experience.[47]

General anesthesia provides an even sharper edge. Rather than shutting the brain down, anesthetic drugs reversibly alter consciousness by disrupting the functional connectivity of cortical networks (especially frontoparietal and thalamocortical circuits) so that integrated, reportable experience temporarily disappears even as neural activity continues.[48] Patients typically “wake up” with no memory of the interval, yet we assume the same person went under and came back.

At these edges of deep sleep, anesthesia, and, more finally, death, the continuity of the self becomes precarious. Biological processes and neural activity may persist or resume, but from the first-person point of view there are gaps in experience that force us to ask whether an unbroken, thinking self is something that exists in fact or something we continuously reconstruct from memory once awareness returns. For a metacognitive curriculum, this matters: students are not just “having” experiences; they are constantly stitching them into a story of who they are.

So if a human’s biological body died, but all of their memories were captured and immediately transferred to a clone at the moment of death, are they dead? If a person were to travel back in time to their exact moment ten years ago, without any memories or experience from those ten years, will anything be different? The Ship of Theseus paradox continues adding layers of complexity to conceptualizing identity. If awareness is forever lost upon bodily death, as in that your soul cannot be transferred from body to body, then how many transplants can a person get before they are no longer themselves?

Many people have been lucky and fortunate enough to have their heart replaced with another’s at a time where they would have otherwise died. Ancient Egyptians, Aristotle, Upanishads, and medieval Islamic and Christian philosophers argued cardiocentricism believing that the heart was essentially the command center for the psyche, or soul.[49], [50] If that’s the case, then is a person with a heart transplant the same person she was before the surgery? What about in the middle of the surgery during a heart-lung bypass when a machine takes the role of “animating the body”? Even in less dramatic situations, identity is being revised through puberty, trauma, migration, or just repeatedly hearing “you’re the smart one” or “you’re the troublemaker.”

I give more weight to the brain as being the source of the soul, but the logic applies. As technology and innovation increase at the rapid pace they have been, it would be foolish to assume that a brain transplant is impossible in the future. But until then, I have to ground myself in the technology of the day. Currently, Elon Musk and his team at Neuralink have already connected brain activity to technological devices. Trialists have begun to play video games without moving. Prosthetics are getting closer and closer to achieving full limb replacements by connecting signals to the brain. It’s not long before devices can regain hearing for a deaf person and restore some form of sight to a blind person.

By tweaking these senses, it is not simply providing sight – it is channeling a blind person’s brain to perceive their surroundings in a similar way to a sighted person. When you look at grass, your brain will perceive grass differently than a cow, which will perceive it differently than another blade of grass. You might notice that it’s green or brown, tall or short, or something else. A cow might not know what it is aside from food. Humans are typically trichromats, while cows are dichromats, so the color of grass to them might not be much different than the color of a lake.

For us to look at a piece of grass and form these complex thoughts about it that don’t exist in a cow’s ability to comprehend further proves the complexity of consciousness. A cow will look at grass and see “food” because it’s been programmed to for millennia and millennia. Archeologists specializing in the Cognitive Revolution of 75,000 years ago agree that consciousness, by our understanding, is unique to humans. We are so far the only collection of atoms with the ability to communicate and comprehend abstract ideas. Our brains are able to tap into that extra realm and choose to analyze the structure and qualities of the grass.

Endospection, then, is the metacognitive habit of internalizing and examining self-identity. I picture this work on the self as happening in and around a pulsing sphere of identity. I call that sphere the Endosphere: the current, always-changing configuration of who we take ourselves to be. Endospection names the habit of returning to, narrating, and revising that Endosphere over time. It is the disciplined practice of asking:
Who is the “I” doing this thinking?
How have my body, memories, technologies, and social labels helped build the story I call “myself”?
Which parts of that story feel given, and which have I chosen, or could I choose, to change?

In a school context, endospection is not an abstract thought experiment; it is the foundation for students monitoring their own learning, biases, and decisions. A curriculum that treats self-identity as fixed or invisible leaves that story to be written by accident: by algorithms, stereotypes, and whoever yells the loudest. A curriculum that centers endospection treats self-identity as the first object of study, giving students the tools to notice, question, and revise the narratives through which they think, learn, and act.

Students should not depend on curriculum evaluation tools or direction from others to decode the existence of a hidden curriculum. Because it is impossible to teach all of history, many high schools continually attempt to fit as much knowledge into lessons as possible. Still, some teachers find themselves rushing to cram the last four decades of content into the final weeks of the year. The content-driven approach forces dependency on being told what to learn next, sacrificing the metacognitive habit of forming relationships between internal nodes of knowledge. Endospection pushes in the opposite direction: instead of training students to wait for the next unit, it trains them to notice and build connections among what they already know and who they already are.

Another limitation endospection resolves comes from a critical misunderstanding in content-first curriculum: it treats both history and identity as fixed facts to be delivered, rather than as stories that are constantly revised as the future unfolds. A curriculum that does not recognize that the future affects the past cannot easily accept individual growth and evolving identities. A core aspect of endospection is that both knowledge and identity are fluid and ever changing. Both on a societal and individual level, across two moments or two millennia, the values of individuals (which collectively form the values of society) fluctuate.

Less than five centuries ago, or around twenty generations ago, geocentrism was the dominant belief; the reality for sixteenth-century peasants and emperors, farmers and kings, was simply that the earth was the center of existence. Without a comprehension of the universe, gravity, rotation, or astrophysics, that was reality. History curriculum is rewritten every generation; as historiography changes, different interpretations of historical realities shed new light on entire foundations. Endospective practice makes this explicit for students: what feels like “reality” in one moment may later be understood as one interpretation among many.

How will future generations view us? Will our reality of current events be similar to the reality taught in classrooms two hundred years from now? Will our reality of current events be similar to our recollection of this time ten years from now? Without a persistent photographic memory, and without being able to recreate the exact conditions under which an event happened, all that is left is the concept or takeaway. Even with written, photographic, or video evidence, the recreation of the moment becomes limited by one’s current endospection; we do not return to the event itself, but to the event as refracted through who we have become.

For teachers, endospection means designing tasks that explicitly ask students to revisit their own prior thinking, compare it to their present perspective, and name what changed and why. For students, it means developing the habit of noticing how new experiences, new information, and new futures reshape the stories they tell about themselves and their world – rather than assuming that “who I am” and “what really happened” were settled long ago.

Intentional control and ownership over one’s reality is a product of a metacognitive curriculum. This control and ownership is forged through practice, preparation, and prediction. While it is not necessary to carve out special time for endospection (endospection is possible in every moment) intentional and productive awareness of it should be offered to students in the form of structured opportunities.

Endospection is not simply answering direct questions such as “What are my values?” or “What are my thoughts regarding my political identity?” While there are aspects of metacognition embedded in these questions, they remain cognitively surface-level; the emphasis is on the what. Endospection invites further exploration into the why and how. More important questions become “How do I incorporate my values in my daily life?” or “Why do I value honesty?”

Other opportunities to engage in metacognitive endologue[51] can be more indirect. A class project might encourage students to design an autobiography where the medium itself reflects their sense of self. This added dimension not only allows for differentiated journeys and outcomes; it also directs endospection as students decide how to represent their lives. One student who is musically gifted might compose a four-part arrangement, transposing the key or tempo to mimic different parts of their life. Another student might code a digital scrapbook with animation, designing the horizontal and vertical flow along axes of their values.

There is no floor to the depth of exploration of self-identity. With each new experience, one’s understanding of reality is altered. Without the opportunity to explore how new ideas affect old ideas, students are left in a confused state, hoping that their recall and memorization abilities will get them an A. Not only does our understanding of knowledge change, but so do our values. Even the foundations from which those values emerge reconstruct over time. Opportunities for students to continue exploring their own identity through metacognitive endospection are effectively endless.

omnipere-impl.text: At some point in their schooling, students inevitably endologue questions such as, “Why do I have to learn this?” or “When will I ever use this?” The unfortunate presumptive reality regarding the perception of schools incites student trepidation. When correctness is treated as pre-determined and the curriculum is framed as something already justified, students learn, often unconsciously, to subordinate their curiosity to institutional expectations.

Omnipere emerges as the antidote: a metacognitive habit that legitimizes wandering, wondering, and intellectual movement without predetermined destinations. It is the practice of allowing thought to travel across disciplines, experiences, identities, and imagined possibilities without first asking whether such travel is required or assessable. In a system that too often trains learners to wait for permission before thinking broadly, omnipere restores the birthright of exploration, treating curiosity not as a distraction from learning but as one of its highest forms.

Omniperegrination names the journey that follows when this habit is activated: the unfolding, recursive movement by which a learner follows a thread of interest wherever it leads, weaving new connections into their evolving reality.

Emphasis on exploration and curiosity is certainly not new in philosophy or education. Omnipere crystallizes several strands of curriculum thought that have long gestured toward exploration but rarely named it as a distinct metacognitive habit.

Dewey’s experimental education positioned experience and inquiry at the heart of schooling. In his cycle of impulse, curiosity, problem, and reflection, genuine learning begins when a puzzling situation interrupts the flow of routine and the learner feels compelled to “try something out.” Exploration, in Deweyan terms, is not ornamental; it is the starting point for thinking. Yet even in Dewey’s most generous formulations, the school day is still structured around teacher-defined problems and subjects. Students may experiment within a frame, but the frame itself is usually not up for renegotiation.

Reconceptualist theorists, especially Pinar, pushed exploration into autobiographical terrain through currere, where the learner revisits past events, imagines possible futures, and interrogates the present to re-narrate their educational life. This is a form of exploration, but it is primarily temporal and reflective while leaning heavily on what I have called endospection: examining how the self has been constructed over time.

More recent student-led and recursive models attempt to place exploration at the center of classroom structure itself. In these designs, students co-create units, generate driving questions, and sometimes even set the sequence of study. The class “recurses” on its own work, using each project as the seed for the next. At the extreme, the teacher becomes facilitator of a curriculum that is almost entirely emergent from student interests.

Omnipere sits in conversation with all three currents but diverges in important ways. With Dewey, it shares the conviction that curiosity is a starting condition of meaningful learning. With currere, it shares an emphasis on identity and autobiographical meaning-making. With student-led designs, it shares a commitment to honoring student questions as legitimate drivers of curricular movement.

But omnipere is one habit among six, not a totalizing model of schooling. It does not ask teachers to abandon structure, nor does it assume that the only “authentic” learning is fully student-run. Instead, it treats exploration as a metacognitive stance that can live inside structured environments and alongside other habits. Where fully emergent approaches sometimes collapse under the weight of boundless choice, omnipere is deliberately bounded: it guarantees the right to wander, but not the obligation to wander all the time.
Because omnipere is the freest of the habits, it is easy to mistake it for things it is not:

First, omnipere is not mere distraction or passive daydreaming. A student staring out the window and mentally replaying last night’s argument may be thinking vividly, but unless a spark of curiosity appears—“How did we get there? Could that have gone differently? What does this say about how I handle conflict?”—the experience has not yet become omniperegrination. Omnipere presumes intentional curiosity: a felt pull to follow a question, pattern, or phenomenon beyond its original frame. A student who cannot control their thoughts, or explore curiosities intentionally, does not omniperegrinate; they only drift.

Second, omnipere is not yet research. Research, as I define it later, is curiosity that has been harnessed toward a goal: it involves framing questions, selecting methods, gathering evidence, and iterating toward some provisional answer or product. Omnipere precedes this. It is the open-ended phase in which the learner allows questions to multiply without demanding that they immediately become answerable or useful. To omniperegrinate is to explore without knowing in advance which inquiries will crystallize into research problems.

Third, omnipere is not the same as critical reflection. Critical thinking and reflection can and should attend to omniperegrinations; they evaluate sources, identify biases, and ask how new ideas fit into or disrupt one’s reality. But omnipere itself does not require closure. One can omniperegrinate without ever arriving at a tidy “why.” The learning happens in the expansion and reconfiguration of the internal knowledge graph: new nodes, new edges, new possible paths between what once seemed unrelated.

For this reason, it is unhelpful to speak of “productive” versus “unproductive” omnipere. Omnipere, by definition, is productive: the moment exploration becomes intentional, it is already restructuring the learner’s reality, even if no assignment is finished and no conclusion is written down. The more meaningful contrast is between omniperegrination and its counterfeits: algorithmic wandering, compliant busywork disguised as choice, or “student voice” narrowed to pre-approved options.

Consider a student in an art class who notices that two pigments, when blended, create a surprising shade. Omnipere begins with a simple, honest question: Why does that color look like that? From there, omniperegrination might unfold along a chain like this:
The student wonders how light interacts with pigment and begins reading or watching videos about wavelengths, absorption, and reflection.

This leads to curiosity about how different creatures perceive color: humans as trichromats, some animals as dichromats or tetrachromats. “Color” is no longer just paint on a canvas but a biologically contingent, species-specific phenomenon.
From there, the student begins thinking about other invisible structures like sound waves, radio signals, Wi-Fi, cosmic radiation. What else exists in the room that cannot be seen?
That, in turn, raises questions about invisible realities in religion or philosophy: spirits, forces, energies, karma. How do cultures name and interpret what cannot be directly perceived?
This curiosity then drifts toward dimensionality: how might a two-dimensional being understand a three-dimensional world, and what does that metaphor suggest about the limits of human perception?
The student finds resources on string theory’s higher dimensions and starts connecting 2D art, 3D space, and speculative multidimensional models.
The initial “why does this color appear this way?” may never be fully resolved in a formal sense. But the student has:
encountered new conceptual tools (wavelength, spectrum, perception),
developed new metaphors for invisible structure, and
connected art to physics, philosophy, and cosmology.

Their internal reality has shifted; the network of concepts through which they understand the world is more complex and more flexible. That is omniperegrination: not a straight line from question to answer, but an intentional wandering through adjacent possibilities.

In classic public schooling, the ability to omniperegrinate like this is often limited to the content within the course. In a typical middle school art class, the syllabus will not include objectives around sound waves, religious metaphors, or higher dimensions. The links between 2D geometric constructions in math, 2D composition in art, and higher-dimensional models in physics rarely surface. Omnipere names the habit that notices those possible connections and begins walking them anyway.

Omniperegrination can be as narrow or as wide as a student’s intentional curiosity allows. It can remain strictly within a discipline or stretch across many. The key variable is not the breadth of the journey but the learner’s stance toward it.
Take welding. At first glance, it appears purely technical: amperage, heat, bond strength, metallurgy, safety protocols. But welding can become a grounding point for omniperegrination:
A student might begin by wondering why certain metals fuse more easily than others, leading to questions about atomic structure and chemical bonding.

From there, the concepts of joining, tension, fracture, and solidifying may begin to operate as metaphors: how do relationships hold or break, how do communities fuse or split, how do ideas become “fixed” or remain malleable?
Soldering two wires together to form a new circuit becomes an image for creating partnerships, writing policy that binds groups, or composing music that welds discordant themes into a coherent whole.

At that point, the omniperegrination has moved from strictly technical understanding to abstract and fluid meaning-making. The act of welding is still itself, there is no requirement to turn shop class into a philosophy seminar. But it has become a node connected to a much wider network of ideas. The student has not necessarily “answered” a defined research question, yet their capacity to think with and through welding has expanded.
In this sense, omnipere does not require schools to abandon practical, content-specific learning. It invites teachers to treat each domain as a launchpad rather than a cage.

curriculum-fences.text: Content-specific structure is not inherently “bad.” Courses, schedules, and syllabi exist for reasons that are not purely oppressive. They can protect students from chaos, ensure access to foundational knowledge, and make shared discourse possible. What becomes corrosive is when content structure is treated as the foundation of education rather than as scaffolding built around deeper habits like omnipere and endospection.

Even though omnipere operates on a more abstract, conceptual dimension than cognitive exploration within a single subject, it does not float above content. It uses content as raw material. Omniperegrination moves through art, physics, welding, literature, history, and every other subject or field. That is why this book does not discard subjects or communication; there are five other habits and a three-dimensional compass (explained later) that attend to structure, assessment, and socially accepted “truths.” Omnipere’s distinct contribution is to break from the assumption that structure is the starting point, and instead position structure as one possible anchor for curiosity.

autonomy-power.text: The goal of this (and the other) habit(s) is to prevent one’s reality from being silently suppressed or flattened by dominant narratives, individual biases, or narrow definitions of what counts as legitimate thinking. Omnipere works by building relationships between past and new nodes of thought, ideas, beliefs, perceptions, curiosities, and events (both autobiographical and external). It is a form of autonomous thought: opportunities can be provided by teachers, institutions, or peers; guidance and structure can be present; collaboration can shape the journey. But the actual omniperegrination happens within the learner’s own cognitive landscape and is as fluid as endospection.

A student who has had repeated opportunities to omniperegrinate develops a reality with more internal room. That expanded internal reality directly strengthens what I later call exospection: the habit of understanding and acting within the realities of others. When learners are practiced at noticing and re-routing their own thinking, following threads across domains, and integrating new perspectives into their graph of meaning, they are better equipped to recognize that other people’s realities are likewise complex, layered, and in motion. In that sense, omnipere is not a luxury add-on to a content curriculum. It is one of the most effective ways to expand exospection and, by extension, to support democratic, anti-oppressive education.

Endospection and Omnipere together define the inner landscape of metacognition in this model: who I am, and how my thinking is allowed to travel. The remaining habits take that inner mobility and connect it to evidence, evaluation, other people’s realities, and public action. By legitimizing intentional exploration as a core metacognitive habit, schools can help students resist being trapped inside a single, imposed way of understanding the world and instead cultivate the capacity to move through many.

noema-constellations.text: Up to this point, I have been describing the first two habits of a metacognitive curriculum through a pulsing sphere of selfhood and particles of controlled wander. I call that sphere the Endosphere: the current, always-changing configuration of who we take ourselves to be. Endospection names the work we do on that Endosphere – the ongoing habit of revisiting our own story, testing and revising the meanings we give to our experiences, and noticing how our sense of “who I am” shifts over time.

From the surface of the Endosphere, small units of meaning are constantly being produced. Whenever an experience stands out like a sharp comment, a memorable line, a solved equation, or a disturbing headline, a part of it becomes a discrete unit we can, in principle, return to. I call these units noema.[53] A noema can be as simple as “2 + 2 = 4,” as complex as “the summer I almost drowned,” or as general as “people with power usually cannot be trusted.” What matters for this curriculum is that a noema can separate from the Endosphere, move, combine with other noema, and later be recalled, reinterpreted, or let go.

Omnipere and its unfolding, omniperegrination, describe a particular stance toward these noema. Instead of fixing them into conclusions right away, the learner allows them to move. Noema emerge from the Endosphere and drift in cognitive space. Some stay close, others move farther away. They bump into each other, sometimes form loose clusters, and sometimes drift apart again. Over time, some clusters become denser and start to pull in additional noema. From the learner’s point of view, these denser regions feel like recurring themes or hunches: experiences around fairness and discipline at school, an ongoing interest in maps, a persistent worry about climate, or a repeated curiosity about why certain rules in math always seem to work. Omnipere does not require that these patterns be named or finalized. It simply ensures that the wandering is intentional and that noema are given a chance to connect.

However, wandering alone does not answer the question of what to do with these patterns. At some point, a learner has to decide which clusters of noema are worth deeper attention and how to follow them up. Not every cluster needs the same level of focus. This is where the next habit enters: Constellare.

constellare-impl.text: Before Constellare is a habit, it is an image. Imagine vertical blue poles extending outward from different points on the Endosphere into the space where noema drift. Each pole represents a guiding question, purpose, or concern strong enough to pull nearby noema into a more organized arrangement. When a pole appears, noema that were previously scattered begin to move into orbit around it. Loose clusters tighten. Patterns that first appeared during omniperegrination become clearer and more stable. A region of the learner’s internal “sky” starts to look less like random points and more like a constellation.

Constellations, in this sense, are not just discoveries; they are constructions. A group of stars becomes “Orion” only after someone draws a shape through them and decides that shape matters. The same is true of noema. Omnipere can lead to spontaneous clusters (moments when previously separate experiences suddenly feel linked), but Constellare is the habit of treating those clusters as objects of inquiry. It is the purposeful organization of noema around a “so what?” question such as: What do I do with this belief? How do I make sense of this pattern? Why does this cluster of experiences matter enough to investigate?

Constellare differs from both Endospection and Omnipere in how much it commits the learner. Endospection focuses on describing and revising the Endosphere itself. Omnipere focuses on following noema and noticing emerging connections. Constellare focuses on selecting, organizing, and working with those connections. When a learner omniperegrinates, they follow noema with curiosity, letting them suggest new directions without requiring an immediate outcome. In Constellare, the flow reverses: the learner starts from a question or purpose and uses it to organize the noema. The blue pole rises from the Endosphere because something about this cluster relates to who the learner is or who they might become. In this model, research is not defined primarily by formal methods, but by the habit of Constellare: bringing noema together into constellations that are strong enough to be examined, questioned, revised, and used.

At this stage, the work of Constellare is mostly endologue. Its primary audience is the self. Students may draw simple diagrams, annotate texts, map their own experiences, build basic lists or tables, or take notes that no one else sees. The key move is not yet external presentation (that will be the focus of Exospection) but internal organization. How am I arranging my noema so they make sense to me? How am I using whatever research tools I have to answer my own “so what?” before I worry about explaining it to anyone else?

constellare-opp.text: For curriculum design, Constellare raises a different set of questions than Endospection and Omnipere. If Endospection asks, “How does this unit give students tools to examine who they are?” and Omnipere asks, “Where in this unit are students allowed to wander and connect ideas on their own terms?”, Constellare asks: “Where, when, and how does this unit support students in turning wandering into research?” A metacognitive curriculum cannot assume that this transition will happen automatically. It must build in structures where students are prompted to choose a cluster of noema, frame a “so what?” question, and organize evidence or experiences around that question in a deliberate way.

In a conventional content-first design, it is easy to tuck Constellare back inside familiar boxes: “research in history,” “inquiry in science,” “projects in welding.” That is not the architecture I am proposing. In a metacognitive curriculum, the primary unit of design is not the subject but the opportunity. A structured opening for students to exercise habits like Endospection, Omnipere, and Constellare with sufficient depth and support. Content still matters, but curriculum should incorporate it not because it belongs to “ninth-grade history,” but because it offers rich noema to constellate.

From this perspective, Constellare does not live inside history or science classes; those categories are secondary, if they appear at all. Instead, a term or year is built from a sequence of interdisciplinary opportunities, each framed around a theme or problem that invites students to turn clusters of noema into constellations. Knowledge from history, science, literature, or technical fields enter as sources of noema (cases, data, stories, tools) that students draw on as needed for their constellaration.
You can imagine a few types of opportunities that make this concrete:

Opportunity: Evidence and Power.Students begin by omniperegrinating through examples of how decisions get justified in different arenas: court cases, school discipline policies, public health campaigns, family rules, religious teachings, scientific debates. These are not “units” from different subjects; they are all sources of noema around the same theme. Constellare begins when students identify a cluster that already matters to them (say, moments when authority is used to punish vs. to protect) and frame a “so what?” question such as, When is punishment treated as justice, and by whom? The curriculum then provides research supports (interview protocols, document analysis tools, basic statistics, media literacy frameworks) and dedicated time for students to organize the noema they collect into constellations they can examine and revise.

Opportunity: Change Over Time.Here the shared theme is not “history content” but the idea of transformation across time. Students might encounter ecological succession, urban gentrification, language change, personal habit formation, and constitutional amendment not as separate subjects, but as parallel cases. Omnipere allows noema to collect around whichever examples strike a nerve. Constellare asks students to choose one cluster (perhaps “how neighborhoods change and for whom”) and build a constellation that cuts across disciplines: archival photos, census data, oral histories, zoning maps, public health reports, topographical data, and their own Endospective reflections about place.

Opportunity: Perception and Reality.Students are given access to noema from optics and color theory, illusions in art, cognitive biases in psychology, religious or philosophical concepts of the unseen, and the physics of waves and fields. Omniperegrination might lead some toward visual art, others toward technology, others toward spirituality. Constellare is the moment when each learner chooses a guiding question “What can’t we see but still shapes our lives? or When should we doubt our own perception?” and then organizes a constellation of noema drawn from across these domains to answer it for themselves.

In each case, the curricular center is not a discipline but an opportunity to constellate: a designed space where students move from scattered curiosity to organized noema anchored in a “so what?” that matters to their Endosphere. Teachers do not ask, “What content standards must I cover this semester?” so much as, “What opportunities am I building for Constellare, and what kinds of noema will students need access to in order to do that work?”

constellare-design.text: Seen this way, a Constellare task is not just “write a research paper.” It has four design commitments:

Start from clusters, not topics.The task begins by surfacing existing clusters of noema through Endospective and Omnipere activities: journaling, discussion, media exploration, lived experiences. Students choose a cluster that already has gravity for them, rather than being handed a generic topic.

Frame a genuine “so what?”Students are supported in turning that cluster into a guiding question or purpose that links their internal reality to something beyond it: understanding, decision-making, design, or action. The curriculum treats this framing as real work, not a throwaway prewriting step.

Supply diverse noema, not a single canon.Instead of marching through a fixed content sequence, the opportunity offers a range of potential sources—across fields, media, and perspectives—so that different constellations are possible. Content is curated for its capacity to interact with students’ noema, not because it belongs to “this course.”

Make the constellation visible.Students externalize their Constellare: concept maps, annotated collections, codebooks, timelines, design briefs, or other structures that show how their noema are being organized. These artifacts become the basis for feedback, Refraction (interrogating biases and blind spots), and later Exospection (sharing and negotiating meaning with others).

Where many forms of project-based learning still begin from discipline standards and then add a “driving question,” an opportunity-centered, Constellare-first curriculum flips the sequence. It begins from noema and themes—what is actually present in students’ Endospheres and experiences—and then pulls in disciplinary methods and content as needed to support their constellations. The “project” is not a vehicle for sneaking in content; the content is a vehicle for strengthening Constellare.

Section 7: Designing a Metacognitive Curriculum
7.0 Introduction: The Illusion of Difference
The Homogeneity of Schools: Despite surface differences (funding, location), the architecture of American schooling is identical: age-graded cohorts, bell schedules, and the "Core Four" subjects.

The "Regular Learner" Myth:The explosion of IEPs and 504s proves the current model is broken. We treat unique cognition as a "disability" requiring legal accommodation, rather than the default human reality.
Argument: We don’t need a system that accommodates exceptions; we need a system where cognitive variation is the standard.
7.1 The Central Question: If Not Content, Then What?
(This subsection directly addresses your uncertainty. It defines the terms.)
The Vacuum: If we remove "Content Coverage" as the anchor, what fills the void?
The Answer: We shift from Content (the input) to Metacognition (the processor), using Opportunities (the environment) to get there.

Why Metacognition? (The "Operating System" Argument):The Volatility of Content: Facts change. History is rewritten. Technology evolves. If school is only about "downloading" content, students become obsolete the moment the world changes.
The Stability of Metacognition: "Learning how to learn" is the only skill that survives technological acceleration.

The Critical Distinction: A "Unit on the Civil War" teaches a specific narrative. A "Unit on Refraction (Bias) using the Civil War" teaches the student how to navigate any conflicting narrative they encounter in the future.

Why is a "Unit of Metacognition" just as important as practical knowledge?Practical knowledge (the "App") creates immediate utility. Metacognition (the "OS") ensures the system doesn't crash when the environment changes. Without the OS, the App is useless.
7.2 The Mechanism: "Opportunities" Instead of Assignments
(Why you designed it this way)
The Design Rationale:Current curricula act like "thermometers" (measuring specific knowledge) but actually function as "thermostats" (controlling/limiting what is learned).
The Shift: We stop designing "Assignments" (tasks to prove you consumed content) and start designing Opportunities (spaces to practice thinking).
The 3D Opportunity Compass:Why this structure? To prevent the curriculum from collapsing into a single "efficient" corner. Most schools heavily favor Structured, Practical, Independent work.
The Goal: A balanced diet. To force the curriculum to offer opportunities in the "neglected" corners (Theoretical, Flexible, Collaborative).
7.3 The Core Architecture: The 6 Metacognitive Nodes
(Here are the specific objectives for each node, answering "What is the goal?")
Node 1: Endospection (Self-Identity)Objective: To map one's own internal cognitive architecture.
Goal: Internal Stability. "Who do I think I am, and why?" Unlearning imposed narratives to build a secure base for inquiry.
Node 2: Diffusion (Exploration)Objective: To engage in pure, unrestricted curiosity without an agenda.
Goal: Expansion. Embracing the butterfly effect of learning; finding the "unknown unknowns".
Node 3: Vectoring (Research)Objective: To give magnitude and direction to curiosity.
Goal: Precision. Turning wandering wonder into targeted inquiry; mastering the tools of sourcing and retrieval.
Node 4: Refraction (Critical Thinking/Bias)Objective: To analyze how identity and context bend information.
Goal: Truth Maintenance. Recognizing that new information forces updates to internal reality; managing bias rather than denying it.
Node 5: Exospection (Collaboration)Objective: To map external minds and contexts.
Goal: Empathy & Communication. Understanding stakeholder biases; fitting others' realities into your own to ensure communication is received.
Node 6: Synthesis (Application/Creation)Objective: To create entirely new ideas by combining previous nodes.
Goal: Novelty. Not summarizing existing knowledge, but constructing something that didn't exist before.
7.4 The Structure: The Rotating "Subject Bubbles"
Breaking the Silos: Instead of "Math Class," students enter "Subject Bubbles" (e.g., a "Vectoring" bubble might use Biology content; a "Refraction" bubble might use History content).
The Role of the Facilitator:K–5 (Pedagogical Mentors): Focus on Endospection and Structure (Hierarchy Model).
6–12 (Subject Matter Experts): Focus on Synthesis and Theory (Orrery Model). They model passion and expertise, while the AI handles the "living portfolio" of content tracking.

The act of ‘knowing’ is an epistemological challenge when using static communication. When knowledge is viewed through the collection of brute facts for application, rather than the relational applications of changing ‘facts’, learning becomes corrupt and oppresses the learner. Two methods of meditation display the two distinct camps philosophers seek out relational knowledge. The first of which is Rene Descartes’s Cogito. In this camp, knowledge can only arise from doubting. The more you doubt, the more you know what you do not know. Broken down completely, there is only but one truth: “I think therefore I am.” While Descartes tried to strip everything away to find the one isolated truth, Dewey argues that isolation is the enemy of knowledge. We only know things by connecting them to other things. This is how meaning is made and how objective objects become ‘enriched’Yet both philosophies of ‘knowing’ share the same foundation of facts being relational. Therefore, 'to know' is not to find an unmovable bedrock; it is to maintain a stable graph of relationships. When a new node is introduced (e.g., a new historical perspective), the relationship changes, and what we 'knew' must be revised. I use the term endologue (from the Greek endon, meaning “within,” and logos, meaning “discourse” or “reason”) to distinguish this process from a standard monologue. While an internal monologue is often static or performative, a recounting of what one already knows, an endologue is dynamic. It refers to a recursive internal dialectic where the learner questions, evaluates, and evolves their own cognitive structures. It is not merely talking to oneself; it is the active restructuring of one’s reality through self-conversation. ↑

I use the term omnipere (from Latin omnis, meaning “all,” and peregrinari, meaning “to wander or travel through unknown territory”) to name the metacognitive habit of boundaryless exploration. Whereas ordinary curiosity is often constrained by task, discipline, or expectation, omnipere signifies a liberatory wandering—intellectual, imaginative, and experiential—across all domains of thought. The learner moves fluidly between the inner landscape of identity, the outer landscape of the world, and the conceptual landscapes that arise between them.I use the extended form omniperegrination to emphasize the processual nature of this wandering. If omnipere is the disposition, omniperegrination is the journey itself—the unfolding, recursive movement by which learners pursue emerging questions, destabilize assumptions, and expand the range of what they believe possible. It is not aimless drifting but the freedom to follow thought wherever it leads, cultivating ownership over one’s own thinking. ↑

Noema are “neither an object nor a part of an object,” but a complex that includes “every factor determining the meaning of noetic activity” (p. 437).
